We invite attention to the underneath j w þÿextrac from . a Eondon Paper, and we rejoict that the following principles have been settled by the decision of the Courts in reference to the legal responsibilities of subscribers : þÿ þÿ 1. Subscribers who do not give express notice to the contrary are considered as wishing to continue their subscriptions. 2. It subscribers order the discontinuance of their periodicals, the publisher may send them till all arrearages are paid; and subscribers are responsible for all the numbers sent. 3. It subscribers neglect or refuse to take their periodicals from tiie office to which they i are directed, they are held responsible till they have settled their hills, and ordered their periodicals to he discontinued. Sending numbers hack, or leaving them in the otlice, is not such notice of discontinuance as the law requires. 4. If subscribers remove to other places without informing the publishers, and their periodical is sent to the former direction, they are field responsible. 5. The Courts have decided that refusing to lake a new spaper or periodical from the office, or removing and leaving it uncalled for until arrearages are paid, is jtrima faeie evidence ofintentional þÿfraud. That the above law has been acted upon in the United States, the following from the New York Tribune, clearly shews : þÿ þÿ The liability of subscribers to newspapers and periodicals, is not. in many cases duly considered. A case has recently been decided, which will

awaken attention on the subject. The publisher took no notice of this, nor of several subsequent notices of refusal to take tiie paper from the Post-office. The result was, that noth withstanding the Rhode Islander did not receive t lie paper for several years, yet he was forced to pay Mr. Warding the whole amount

Great curiosity has been felt to see the reply of the Austrian Minister to þÿWebster s famous electioneering despatch about the agent sent to Hungary. We give below a translation of this remarkable document: þÿ (From the Austrian Gazette, September 15, 1851.) Reply of the Chevalier Hulsemann, Austrian Charge de Affaires at the Court at Washington, to his Excellency Daniel Webster, Secretary of Slate of the United States of America. Austiian Legation, July 4, 1861. The undersigned, Charge de Affaires of His Majesty the Emperor of Austria, having submitted to the Emperor your þÿExcellency s right despatch, bearing date Dec 21, 1850, has been instructed to make the following reply : þÿ The conduct of the United States, of which the undersigned had heretofore complained, in sending an agent to Hungary to open a communication with the rebels there in arms then against His Majesty the Emperor, appears to be justified in the said despatch on the ground that the United States are the representatives of purely popular principles of þÿgovernment, principles on which the Governments of those Slates are þÿ themselves wholly founded whence a just and rightful sympathy on the part of the people and Government of the United States on behalf of all movements, wherever and by whomsoever made, in behalf of liberty and equality. Whether, if such truly were the foundation of the American Government, it would justify the course of conduct of which the Emperor

complains, it is not necessary now to inquire, since this assumption on the part of the American Governments to be wholly founded þÿ þÿupon, and þÿ to he the representatives of purely popular principles of þÿgovernment. does not seem to the Emperor to rest on any sufficient foundation. Your Excellency can hardly fail to be aware that in two of the United States, to Vvit, South Carolina and Mississippi, the majority of the inhabitants are kept in a state of degrading personal servitude, with total prohibition of political and social rights, utterly unknown in any portion of the Austrian dominions; that in 14 out of the 111 States, the same is the case with a very large portion of the native-born inhabitants; that even those Stales in which this system does not exist are pledged to support it in the others; for which purpose the General Government is the instrument and agent þÿ a function without the perpetual discharge of which, as no one knows better than your Excellency, especially in the scrupulous return of all refugees from servitude, the Union could not continue to exist. Your Excellency has been pleased to quote the Laybach Circular of May, 1841, as if to illustrate some marked distinction between the principles of the Austrian and the American Governments. The following is the passage quoted : þÿ þÿ Useful and necessary changes in legislation and administration ought only to emanate from the free will and intelligent conviction of those whom God has rendered responsible
for power, All that deviates from this level

(Q ATI 3% leads to disorder, commotions, and evils far more insufferable than those which they pretend to þÿremedy. And can your Excellency say that there is any doctrine here laid down not perfectly consistent with the principles and practice of the American Government? Does your Excellency admit any right on the part of the slaves þÿ that is to say, the large majority of the native population of South Carolina þÿ to rise against and to overturn the rule of their white masters ? Is not the Government of the United States pledged to interfere to put down any such insurrection ? Do not the slaveholders of South Carolina, and of the other States, claim to hold their power directly from God, and to be responsible to Him alone for exercise? And do they not rely on the Bible to prove it ? The undersigned begs leave to entertain the opinion, and he boldly appeals to the j civilized world for the justice of it, that the of the Emperor of Austria to decide alone and exclusively upon the political changes necessary and proper to be made in Hungary is at least as good as the title of n hundred thousand American slaveholders to keep in sole dependence upon their will and pleasure upwards of three millions of their fellow countrymen, while they reduce the remaining twenty millions of nominal freemen to the hardly more enviable condition of slave-drivers and slave-hunters. As to the exercise of this power, claimed in both cases to be of divine origin, the Emperor of Austria has not yet found it neces-

sary to prohibit, under severe penalties, the teaching any portion of his subjects to read and write. On the other hand all Austrian parents are required by law to send their children to school to be instructed in these necessary accomplishments. The Emperor of Austria is no enemy to popular right. He reigns over the people of Austria, for their good, not for Ins own. He is willing to receive light in the discharge of his august duties from every quarter. But he does not look for information þÿ on the great ideas of responsibility and purely popular principles of þÿgovernment to the representatives of an aristocracy of slaveowners, very similar in one respect to that insurgent aristocracy lately suppressed in Hungary, that of preaching democracy with their tongues, while their whole lives consist in the daily exercise over their fellow men of arbitrary power in the most repugnant forms. But although the Emperor cannot in anywise admit the pretentions of the United States to be þÿ the representatives of purely popular principles of þÿgovernment, he has no objection that the relations of the two Governments should stand upon that basis of mutual interference with the internal concerns of each other on which the American Government seems disposed to place it. In corn- j mon with the rest of Christendom, he has long regarded with hearty commisseration the degraded servitude, as it seems to him, disgracelul to Christianity, in which so large a portion of the common people are kept ;

and he cannot doubt that the uprising before long of some black Kossuth will furnish him with an opportunity of carrying these new principles laid down by the American Government into practice, and thereby serving the cause of human happiness, ever dear to the þÿEmperor heart. s Having thus communicated the sentiments of His Majesty on your late despatch, 1 em-

brace this opportunity to renew to your Excellency assurances of my high consideration. HULSEMANN. To his Excellency Daniel Webster, .Secretary of State of the United Stales. þÿ »ooo® þÿ Life. þÿ Of all miracles, the most wonderful is that of life þÿ the common, daily life which we carry about with us, and which every where surrounds us. The sun and stars, the blue firmament, day and night, the tides and seasons, are as nothing compared with it. Life þÿ the soul of the world, but for which creation were not ? It is life which is the grand glory of the world ; it was the þÿconsum mation of a creative power, at which the morning stars sang together for joy. Is not the sun glorious, because there me living eves to be gladdened by his beams 1 is not the fresh air delicious, because there are living creatures to inhale and enjoy it? are not odours fragrant and sounds sweet, and colours gorgeous, because there is the living sensation to appreciate them? Without hie, what were they all ? What were a Creator h;n self, without life þÿ intelligence- understate, ing þÿ to know and adore Him, and to tr»e« His linger in the works that he hath marie 7 Boundless vanity and perpetual change are exhibited in the living beings around ns Take the class of insects alone : of these, not fewer than 100.000 distinct species are a! ready known and described ; and every day is adding to the catalogue. Wherever yea penetrate, that life can he sustained, you find living beings to exist ; in the depths of ocean,

in the arid desert, or at the icy polar regions. The air teems with life. The soil whiih clothes the earth all round, is swarming wuh life, vegetable and animal. Take a drop of water, and examine it with a microscope: lo! it is swarming with living creatures. Within life exists other life, until it recedes before the powers of human vision. The parasitic animalcule, which preys upon or within the body of a large animal, is itself proved upon by parasites peculiar to itself. JSo minute are living animalcules, that Ehrenburg has computed that no fewer than 500.000.000 can subsist in a single drop of water, and each of these monads is endowed with its appropriate organs, possesses spontaneous power of motion, and enjoys an independent vitality. During how many thousands of years has the vitality of seeds been preserved deep in the þÿearth b s osom ! Not less wonderful is the fact slated by Lord Lindsay, wbo took from the hand of an Egytian mummy a tuber, which must have been wrapped up there more than 2.000 years before. The re-establishment of the old Provincial Diets, as well in Schleswig as in Holstein, is conceded by the Danish Government, but under the condition that it is not the last existing Diet that is to be summoned again; that Diet is to be declared dissolved by royal decree, and a new election for another taken, according to the Election Law of 1814, with the exclusion of the vote possessed by the House of Augusteniiurg. 2. That the Danish Government regards the Diet to be thus summoned as one ail interim only, and called for the special purpose of framing an entirely new law of election. 3. That the former connexion between the Duchies for administrative and judicial purposes shall not be again established, but that each Duchy shall have its own administration and its own supreme tribunal. 4. That This evening at about D þÿo clock, ration the resolution of the 17l!i of Sep- on the part of tin Diet of the Confedetember, 1840, reserving to the Diet a competence to maintain the right of the Duchy of Holstein to a closer connexion with the Duchy of Schleswig, shall be regarded as cancelled. After the abolition of the administrative and judicial connexion none of the former institutions common to both of the Duchies
shall continue to exist, except the social nexus of the Ritterschalt.

London Times, January 1C, 1851. FRANCE. (T1Y SUBMARINE TELEGRAPH.) PARIS, Thursday Morning. The President is to preserve his present Title ; he is responsible before the people, to whom he can always appeal. He commands the land and sea forces, lie alone has the initiative of the laws; he has a right to declare the state of siege, referring it to the Senate, lie presents one message every year. Mini- accusation can be brought against No sters but by the Senate. They are only responsible for their respective dulies. The functionaries take the oath of obedience to the constitution and lidelity to the President. In case of the death of the President, the Senate calls upon the nation for a new election. The President has the right, by a secret deed, deposited with the Senate, to designate to the people the citizen whom he recommends to the suffrage, until the election of a new President. The President of the Senate governs jointly with Ministers. The number of senators is not to exceed 150. It is iixed at 80 for the first year. The senators are named for life by the President. Their functions are performed gratuitously. However, the President may grant a salary not exceeding 30,000f. The sitting of the Senate is not to be public. It regulates the constitution of colonies, and all that has not been provided lor by the constitution. It may propose modifications of the constitution, but any modification of the bases laid in the proclamation of December 2 will be referred to universal suffrage. There will be a deputy to the legislative body

for every ,35, 000 electors, elected by universal suffrage for ten years, and receiving no emolument. All adopted amendments are to be sent, without discussion, before the Council of State, and cannot be discussed if not equally adopted by this one. The sittings will last three months. Reports of the sittings by newspapers will be confined to the official reports of the proceedings drawn up by the Bureau. The President and Vice-President are nominated by the President of the Republic for a year. Ministers cannot be Deputies. Petitions may be addressed to the Se- j f nate, but none to the legislative body. The President of the Republic convokes, adjourns, prorogues, and dissolves the legislative body. in case of dissolution, a new one is to be convoked within six months. The Council of State, composed of 40 or 50 members, is nominated and presided over by the President, who may revoke its members. The members receive an

the project of laws, and discuss them before the Legislature. There will be a High Court of Justice, without appeal, before which will be tried all attempts against the State, or its chief. The mayors are appointed by the executive power.

Some years ago there lived in Marseilles an old man uf the name of Guyot ; lie was known to every inhabitant, and every urchin in the streets could point him out as a niggard in his dealings, and a wretch of the utmost penury in his habits of life. From his boyhood, > his old man had lived in the city of Marseilles; and, although the people treated him with scorn and disgust. nothing could induce him to leave it. When he valkcd ibo þÿ tree!0 lie was followed bv a crowd of boys,

3 tt". « !ft <0 It 'JL AT lt3» who, hating him as a grasping miser, hooted him vociferously, insulted him with the coarsest epithets, and sometimes annoyed him by casting stones and tilth at his person. There was no one to speak a kind word in liis favor, no one to bestow an act of friendship, or a nod of recognition upon Guyot. lie was regarded by all as an avaricious, griping old miser, whose whole life was devoted to the hoarding up of gold. At last this object of universal scorn died, and it was found that, by his parsimony, he had amassed an ample fortune. Wiiat was the surprise of his executors, on opening his will, to find these remarkable words : þÿ -Having observed, from my infancy, that the poor of Marseilles are ill-supplied with water, which can only be procured at a great price, 1 have cheerfully labored the whole of my life to procure for them that great blessing, and I direct that the whole of my property shall be expended in building an aqueduct for their use ! þÿ

Many years ago, there lived in a large, cheerless, i and dilapidated old house in St. Petersburg, a wretched I miser. He confined himself to one room, and left the rest of the rambling edifice to moulder into ruin : he cared for no comfort, and deprived himself even of those things which the poorest regard as the necessaries of life ; he seldom lit a fire to repel the dampness, which hung on the wall of his solitary chamber, and a few worthless objects of furniture was all that the room contained. Yet to this singular being the Empress Catherine the Second owed a million of rubles. þÿIIi cellar, it was said, contained casks full of gold, and packages of silver were stowed away in the dismal corners of his ruinous mansion. lie was one of the richest men in Russia. He relied for the safety of his hoards upon the exertions of a huge mastiff, which he had trained to bark and howl throughout the night, to strike terror into the hearts of thieves. The miser outlived the dog; but he disliked to part with any portion of his treasure in the purchase of another cur, and lie resolved to save his money by officiating as bis own watch-dog. Every morning, and every evening, would that insane old man wander about his dismal habitation, barking and howling in imitation of ills recent sentinel.

A miser of the name of Foscue, who had amassed enormous wealth, by the most sordid parsimony, and the most discreditable extortion, was requested by the government to advance a sum of money, as a loan. The miser, to whom a fair interest was not inducement sufficiently strong to enable him to part with his treasured gold, declared his incapacity to meet this demand ; lie pleaded severe losses, and the utmost poverty. Fearing, however, that some of his neighbors, among whom lie was very unpopular, would report his immense wealtli to the government, lie applied ins ingenuity to discover some effectual way oi hiding his gold, should they attempt to institute a search to ascertain the truth or falsehood of Wis pica. With great care and secrecy, he dug a deep cave in his cellar; to this rece ptale for his treasure lie descended by a ladder, and to the trap-door he attached a spring lock, so that, on shutting, it would fasten of itself. By and-by the miser disappeared ; inquiries were made ; the house was searched; woods were explored, and the ponds were dragged ; but no Foscue could they find ; and gossips began to conclude that the miser had fled, with his gold, to some part where, by living incognito, lie 1 could be free from the hands of tlie government. Some time passed on ; the house in which lie had lived was sold, and workmen were busily employed in its repair. In tlie progress of their work they met with the door j of the secret cave, with tlie key in tlie lock outside.

They threw back the door, and descended with a light. Tlie first object upon which tlie lamp was reflected was tlie ghostly body of Foscue tlie miser, and scattered around him were heavy bags of gold, and ponderous chests of untold treasures; a candlestick lay ueside him on the floor. This worshiper of Mammon had gone into his cave, to pay his devoirs to his golden god, and became a sacrifice to ins devotion !

(from Chamber's Edinburgh Journal.) Terrestrial Magnetism. Our knowledge of the laws of magnetism was not increased until 1811, when, on the occasion of a prize proposed by M. Hansteen, whose attention bad for many years been turned to magnetic phenomena, undertook its re-examination. With indefatigable labor M. llansteen traced back the history of the subject, and Idled up the interval from Halley's time, and even from an earlier epoch (1600). The results appeared in ins very remarkable and celebrated work, published in 1810, entitled, " Upon the Magnetism of the Earth in which lie clearly demonstrates, by a great number of facts, the fluctuation which the niagnetical element has undergone during the last two centuries, continuing in great detail the position of llalley þÿ that the whole magnetical system is in motion; that the moving force is very great, extending its effects from pole to pole ; and that its motion is not sudden, but gradual and regular. hi the magnetic atlas which accompanies M. Hansteen's work there is a variation chart for 1787, showing the magnetic force at that period. In this chart the western line of no variation, or that which passes through all places on the

This line of no variation is extremely regular, being almost straight, till it bends round the eastern part of South America, a little south of the equator. The eastern line of no variation is exceedingly irregular, being full of curves and contortions of the most extraordinary kind, indicating plainly the action of local magnetic forces. It hegins in latitude 60® south, below New Holland ; crosses that island through its centre; extends through the Indian Archipelago with a double sinuosity, so as to cross the equator three times þÿ first passing north of it to the east of Borneo, then returning to it, and passing south between Sumatra and Borneo, and then crossing it again south of Cevlori, from which it passes to the east through the Yellow Sea. It then stretches along the coast ot China, making a semicircular sweep to the west, till it reaches the latitude of 71®, when it descends again to the south, and returns northwards with a great semicircular bend, which terminates in the White Sea. Thus it is demonstrated that in the northern hemisphere the general motion of the variation lines is from west to east, in the southern hemisphere from east to

west. Nay, it were better to meet some dangers half-way, though they come nothing near, than to keep too long a watch upon their approaches ; for if a man watch too long, it is odds lie will fall asleep. On the other side, to he deceived with too long shadows þÿ as some have been, when the moon was low and shone on their enemies, and so to shoot off before the time þÿ or to teach dangers to come on, by an over-early buckling toward them, is another extreme. But there are also learned fallacies, and among these we know of no one more common than that which prevails respecting the word education. It is quite usual with lecturers and essayists to derive a profound philosophical meaning from the bare etymology of the term. It is from educo, they tell us, to lead or draw out. It means the drawing out or developing the faculties. It is tlie bringing out the unwrought man, like the polished- statue from the rough hlock of marble. All sorts of changes are rung ' swept upon the word. With some it is the educing of the individuality, with others, of the humanity. Others again talk much of drawing out the ideas, and that, too, without any previous exact i/istruction, or the furnishing of what might be styled þÿ about as wise a course as to attempt Tii develop, or draw out the faculties of a nail-making machine, without ever thinking of putting any well-wrought iron into it. Now, all this is pedantic nonsense. The old Roman Roundheads, from whom the term is derived, never dreamed of any such transcendental conception. The word, in its primary sense, simply means nursing, fostering, rearing. Hence is it afterward applied to knowledge and discipline. It is educed from the simple conception of holding the child hy the iiand, and leading him forth when he first begins to walk. From the same primitive thought comes the word pedagogue, which sim dy means, one who leads a tun/,

and was first applied to the slave, or servant, who conducted the Athenian child to and from school. It would, however, lie hardly worth our while to show the fallacy of this very common etymological deduction, were it not sometimes made the ground of very false ideas. It is to hold a child up, you and lead liitn forth by the hand, before set him to walk alone by himself, r under pretense of developing his faculties, cither of thinking or of locomotion. þÿ Harper's Magazine. From the Dublin University Magazine. Jewish Veneration. The veneration of the Jew for the law the prepared material of thought j is displayed by the grossest superstition, a copy of the Torah or Decalogue being

and hung over the entrance to their chambers, as old crones with us nail a horse-shoe to a door; it is even believed to avail as an amulet or charm capable of averting evil, or curing the most ob- stinate disease. " Ah," said a bed-ridden old Hebrew woman to me, as I visited the mission hospital in Jerusalem, "what can the doctors do for me? If 1 could only touch the Torah I should be made whole." Not exactly comprehending what she meant, I handed her a little tin-cased copy of the Ten Commandments; she grasped it in her emaciated hands, which trembled with anxiety, and her eyes were lit up with a transient gleam of joy. (From tiio London Examiner.) Tlie Australian Colonies. If the comparison between America ind Australia have reference to the facility of achieving and maintaining independence, all the advantages are unquestionably on the side ol Australia. It is at least six times as far away from Europe ; and a military force sufficient to have even a chance of coercing the colonists could not get at them in less than tour months, while the voyage would ton e it to run the gairtilet of the equator and both tropics. \\ hen it reached its destination, supposing its landing to he unopposed, it would have to march every step to seek the insurgents, for there is neither river nor estuary to transport it into the interior of the country. The colonists, ri lie in hand, and driving their docks and herds before them to the privation of the invader, would of course take to the hush, and do so with impunity, being without tents or equipage, or risk of starvation, having a wholesome sky over their heads, and abundant food in their cattle. With a thorough knowledge of localities, the colonial riflemen, under such circumstances, would he more than a match for regular troops, and could pick off soldiers with more ease than they bring down the kangaroo or opossum. We should look, however, to the number and character of the Australian population. In 1828 the total colonial population of Australia was 33,000, of whom a large proportion were convicts. In 148 it was 300,000, of which the con-

victs were but (3000. In the two years since, 37,000 emigrants have proceeded thither, and the total population at this moment can not he less than 330,000. It has, therefore, been multiplied in twenty-two þÿyears time by near seventold; and if it should go on at this rate of increase, in the year 1872 it will amount to close on two millions and a half, which is a greater population than that of the old American colonies at the declaration of independence, and after an existence of 175 years. Such a population, or the one half of it, would, from numbers, position, and resources, be unconquerable. Such is a true picture, we conceive, of the position in which we stand in relation

A T II 3 to our Australian colonies. Meanwhile, the colonists are loyal, affectionate, and devoted, and (the result of absence and distance) with really warmer feelings toward the mother country than those they left behind them. It will he the part of wisdom on our side to keep them in this temper. They demand nothing that is unreasonable þÿ nothing that it is not equally for their advantage and ours that we should promptly and freely concede. They ask for responsible government, and doing so they ask for no more than what is possessed Liy their fellow-citizens. They ought to have perfect power over their own resources and their own expenditure ; hut, in justice and fairness, they ought also to defray their own have litary charges; and, seeing they mineither within nor without any enemy that can cope with a company of light infantry, the cost ought not to he oppressive to them. The Australian colonies are, at present, governed in a fashion to produce discontent and recaleitratiou. They are, consequently, both troublesome and expensive. The nation absolutely gains nothing by them that it would not gain, and even m a higher degree, were they self-governed, or, for that matter, were they even independent. on Thus, tiou to them would go at least ia the emigrasame degree as it does now. It does so go on, to the self-governed colony of Ca- ; nada, and to the country which was once colonies, and this after a virtual separa- | lion of three quarters of a century. In like manner will our commercial

intercourse with the Australian colonies proceed under self-government. In 1828, the whole exports of Australia amounted only to the paltry sum of .£181,000, and in 1815, the last for which there is a return, they had come to .12,187,633, or m seventeen þÿyears time, had been increased by above fourteen-fold, a rapidity ot progress to which there is no parallel. At tins ratio, of course, they can not be expected to proceed in future; for the Australians, having coal, iron, and wool in abundance, will soon learn to make coarse fabrics for themselves. The finer they will long receive From us, as America, after its long separation, still does. But that the Australian Colonies, under any circumstances, are destined to become one of the greatest marts ot British commerce, may he considered as a matter of certainty. The only good market in the world, for the wool, the tallow, the train oil, and the copper ore of Australia, is England; and to England they must come, even if Australia were independent to-morrow; and they must be paid for, too, in British manufactures. Independence lias never kept the tobacco of America from finding its best market in England, nor lias it prevented American cotton from becoming the greatest of the raw materials imported by England. A common lineage, a common language, common manners, customs, laws, and institutions, bind us and our Australian brethren together, and will continue to do so perhaps longer than the British Constitution itself will last. They form

in fact, a permanent bond ol union ; whereas the iulluencc of patronage, and the trickeries of Conservative legislation, do hut provoke and hasten the separation which they are foolishly framed to prevent.

A curious work, entitled, Les Muruilles Revolutionnaircs (Revolutionary Walls), has been published in Paris. It contains the proclamations, decrees, addresses, appeals, warnings, denunciations, remonstrances, counsels, professions of faith, plans of political reconstruction, and schemes of social regeneration, which were stuck on the walls of Paris in the first few þÿmonths agitated existence of the Revolution of 1848. Santo Domingo. translation. (From the þÿ Gaceta de þÿGobierno. ) Miiister of Home Affairs þÿ Cod þÿ Country and Liberty þÿ Dominican Republic. Buenaventura Baez, President of the Republic. Decree establishing Packets between the Republic and St. Thomas.

Considering the importance of regulating in an efficient manner the foreign correspondence þÿ hereby decreed of the Republic, it is Art. 1st. þÿ All merchant vessels undertaking perform the packet service be- to tween the capital and the Island of Saint Thomas, and between Puerto Plata and Saint Thomas, are exempt from all port charges. Art. 2nd. þÿ Vessels desirous of obtaining the privilege stipulated in the foregoing article will require to enter into a formal contract with the Government, or the persons whom it may authorise, as to the manner of performing said service. Art. 3rd. þÿ There will be established provisionally in the capital of the Re- j public, and for account of the Government, two packets between this port and that of St. Thomas, which will sail on the 8th and 23rd of each month. The schooners Mercedes and Buena Centura are destined for this service. Art. 4th. þÿ The said vessels will receive passengers and cargo at all times. Art. 5th. þÿ The General Administrator of the packets will act as the consignee of said vessels, and will be entitled to a commission of five per cent from the nett proceeds thereof. The Government will appoint a consignee in St. Thomas for this service. Art. 6th. þÿ The correspondence to and fro by the packets must be received by the Administrator or Consignees. Art. 7th. þÿ The letters to be deposited in the mail bag of the packets will require to be pre-paid. Art. 8th. þÿ Newspapers are to be free of charge; single letters to pay $2, dou-

ble $4, triple $6 each, and packages $8. Towards the classification of letters either single, double, or triple, the tariff of the Post-office will be taken as a guide. Art. 9th. þÿ The correspondence which comes from St. Thomas by the packets will be subjected to the same charges. Art. 10th. þÿ Passengers by the packets who may carry letters not paid, or who do not deliver the same to the Post-office on their arrival, will be liable to a fine of six Spanish dollars, and the crew will incur a greater penalty (from 12 to 20 dollars fine) according to their station on board. The Alcayde at the port where the infringement will have been discovered will enforce the penalty by a prompt and summary proceeding. Art. 1 1th. þÿ The only letters which will be free from postage by the packets will be the official correspondence of the foreign Consuls, and those of the authorities of the Republic.

Art. 12th. þÿ The present Decree wit; be communicated to the National Con gress, the Secretary of State and Commerce being charged with its execution Given at the National Palace of th< Republic, the 15th February, 1852, and 8th year of Independence. Explosion ok a Powder Magazine þÿ The powder magazine at Loudden, near in Sweden, exploded 24tli ult. The shock shattered several thousand panes of glass in the city of Stockholm, particularly in the Palace. The magazine contained 2800 cwt. of gunpowder, and the loss is esti mated at 115,000 thalers. Two bodies only have been found among the ruins. The following details of the explosion have since been received: þÿ þÿ The shocks were so violent that they shook the earth ; and in several streets broke the windows, and threw open doors, or cast them off' their hinges ; whilst in others pedestrians and even horses were thrown down. The population at first thought there was an earthquake, and rushed to the public squares and open places. Tin terror only ceased when it was announced by placards that the powder maga zinc bad blown up. The magazine was the largcst'in all Sweden, and was situa . ted at half a league from the capital. All that remains of it are some little heaps of ruins. The forest of Liddoc, near which it stood, was ravaged ; trees of several centuries growth and large size were torn up, and carried several hundred yards. A great quantity of the peritoneum was pierced to the extent of ruins of the magazine fell on the Lake of Liddoc, and broke the ice. Some portions of the ruins were found at a distance of two leagues. In the villages of Liddington, Liddingsborg, and others situated beyond the lake, and at a consid crablc distance from the theatre of the þÿilisjnst' the window® wore broken nor

looking glasses, pictures, and other oh- i jects hanging to the wall were thrown down ; and in some houses the walls are damaged, The powder magazine consisted ot four vast buildings, arranged nearly in the form of a cross. It is thought thaflhere were four successive explosions, proceeding from east to west. Fortunately at the time of the catastrophe almost all the workmen had | gone to dinner. Nevertheless it is calculated that more than sixty persons perished. Dead bodies, dreadfully disfigured, and portions of bodies were found at different distances. From a report to the Minister of War by the director of the magazine, it appears the | paddle box lifeboats þÿ magazine contained about 28,500lbs. (280,000?) of gunpowder. The loss, not including the value of the buildings, estimated at 115,000 crowns þÿ 638.000 francs. It appears that the disaster was caused by criminals. The police discovered in a ffole in the earth near the magazine several bundles of chemical matches, a hatchet, a tile, and a hammer, and two liberated convicts named Daniels and Pehrson had been seen hanging about a little þÿbefore. þÿ Ibid.

Cause of Combustion. TO TIIE EDITOR OF TIIE RVBNIXG MAIL. Sir, þÿ Observing that in the statement made by Mr. Jacob Allen, who superintended the fitting of the machinery on hoard the Amazon, relative to the destruction of that vessel, he gives it as his opinion and firm belief that the tire broke out in the starooard fire-store-room, which contained a large quantity ot' tallow, oil, and turpentine ; perhaps the following statement relate e to spontaneous combustion may not be without interest, if it do not lead to the discovery of the cause ot the recent melancholy event: þÿ In the course of the period of my holding the government of Newfoundland,

A 'T 'i Mr. Brooking, a member of one of the greatest commercial firms in that Island, called on me one morning to say that a very serious catastrophe had nearly occurred to their premises, if not to the whole town, by one of their stores having taken lire, the origin of which lie could not discover; that their storekeeper, who had been with them many years, declared that the store was perfectly secure a very short time before, that there was only a cask of linseed oil in it, that before leaving the store he wiped tip a little oil that had escaped from the cask with some tow, which was thrown aside, and immediately left the store, and carefully locked it. Mr. Brooking added that as the negligence of the storekeeper was evident, and his story could not lie a true one. they should be obliged to discharge liitn. On reflecting upon the subject, after that gentleman's departure it. occurred to me that certain oils would with tow or oakum produce, under a certain temperature, spontaneous combustion, and on referring 1o some hooks on chemistry in my possession I found such to he the case, and immediately despatched a messenger for Mr. Brooking, and, communicating to him the above fact, requested that he would make his storekeeper perforin precisely the same operation he had stated himself to have done with regard to wiping up the oil which had leaked from the cask, to use the same material, and throw it in the same place, and then lock the store and superintend the operation himself. Mr. Brooking

did so. From time to time lie looked in at the window, until lie saw a small thread of smoke, which gradually increased until it ultimately burst into a tlanie, and at once solved the question. At this distance of time, I don't remember the exact period the whole operation took, but my impression is, not more than three or four hours. Remembering what a common thing it was on board a ship-off war to wipe up spilt oil with oakum, and even to stop an oil-jar with that material, 1 was strongly impressed with the conviction that many of our ships-of-war which bad never been heard of had met destruction through this practice, and by the first opportunity f despatched full particulars of tin- occurrence to my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty. May it not, Sir, then, lie possible that some spilt oil or turpentine may have been wiped up in a similar manner in the store-room of the Amazon, and that the extreme beat of that part of a steamship produced ignition, and caused the rapid conflagration which has consigned so many souls to an untimely end'/ At all events, being in possession of the abovementioned facts, 1 feel I should not be justified in withholding from you the knowledge of them, and which you can communicate to the public or not, as you may deem the importance to deserve. 1 have the honor to be Sir, your obedient servant, T. COCHRANE, Vice-Admiral. 20, Belgrave-street, Jan. UL

from the Jamaica Des/uitch rclalire to of the 7th " February the follouin g Extract WE cospy from the St. Thomas Times ," St. Thomas; with remarks from the Editor of the Times: þÿ " The packet, due on the 23rd instant, is ajrain lour days beyond her time, and doubts are entertained by many whether she will make her appearance to-day. On the other hand, the inter-colonial steamer destined to take our homeward mails to St. Thomas is due this day, but is not expected to be with us before Saturday. Thus it is that disorder begets disorder, and it is quite apparent that if matters are permitted to continue as they are at present, it will signify little to Jamaica what may be the speed with which the outward mails are conveyed from Southampton to St. Thomas. It is said that the first of the large steamers would leave England either 011 the 17th January, or the 2nd February. So far as we are at present instructed, these vessels will not. he permitted to visit Jamaica, and we shall remain dependent, therelore, as at present, on the inter-colonial steamers for the transfer of our mails and passengers. These vessels, however, have fallen so far back in their work, that unless some step be at once taken to bring them back to their time, all the benefits likely to result from the increased power to be placed on the outward route, will be lost to us, at any rate for some time. It is to be hoped, therefore, that the Company's Superintendent in this City will feel himself justified in

limiting the inter-colonial trip of the steamer, now hourly looked for, so as to enable her to be at her anchorage here in time to take the Mails to be made up on the 7th February, at her appointed hour; and that he will do the same with the steamer that may bring down the 17th January 3Iails. It is only by such a course as this that the time that has been lost can be made good. The Vessels themselves, it is quite clear, have not power to make up the time they have lost, and it would be very vexatious to us in Jamaica to know that our mails, or, what is perhaps of more consequence, our relatives and friends, arc being delayed a week at Ht. Thomas, because the inter-colonial steamers are not there at the proper hour to convey them to us. Both these vessels have now got four days in arrear of their time, and if they cannot make up this arrear by speed, they had better be allowed to start fair once more, and try whether greater regularity can be ensured through the more rapid transit of the outward mails to fit. Thomas. "We do not despair, however, of yet seeing the new steamers coining direct to Jamaica, and we shall only cease to entertain these hopes, when we see the company madly persisting in the adoption of a sand-bank, such as 8t. Thomas, lor the operations of coaling, watering, and provisioning vessels of the heavy tonnage of those lately built by the Company. A steamer, of the tonnage of the " Oronoco," would require to be supplied with probably one thousand tons of coals

for her homeward voyage. þÿ Now, if it takes two days to put something like 150 or 200 tons of coals on board one of the inter-colonial vessels at St. Thomas, we should like to know how so much larger a vessel could be coaled in time to enable her to perform her voyages with regularity. We say nothing of provisions and water, which are notoriously not attainable at St. Thomas. These facts must soon become apparent to the Company, and they must he conclusive of the destination of the steamers. Jamaica, not only from her position on the map, but from her resources, is peculiarly suited to be the central station of the outward

« <© a <© a a: A steamers; and we are convinced that a little experience will prove this. On every account we trust it may be so, and that with the restoration of Jamaica to her proper station on the trunk line of the Company, we may see also the restoration of such a direct line of communication with the Spanish Main as may bring back the trade that has been all but entirely diverted from us." The foregoing article we extract from the confidence we entertain of being competent to refute the whole as ungrounded in its imputations. Our Island is stigmatized as being a sand haul;; such an accusation could emanate only from the pen of one whose travels, like his mind, are confined to a very narrow compass. Our harbour is the first object which attracts the admiration of the stranger; its mouth and all the approaches being of the boldest water, and free from all encumbrance. Private enterprise here, long ago, built two coal depots, with the necessary appurtenances, capable each of coaling Jour steamers at a time, and which, no doubt, together, cost fully one hundred thousand dollars. We are yet to learn of Jamaica building even a tighter for the accommodation of the Royal Mail steamers ! ! ! St. Thomas as an important central point in the Carrihean sea, the London daily papers have before now shewn as clearly as is possible to do, and would only, with us, be a waste of time to recapitulate. The Jamaicans vainly hope that the large steamers may yet go direct to them ; and let us suppose their hopes

gratified : what may we not expect to hear from the Antiguans, Barbadians, Demerarians, Trinidadians, Ac., when such an arrangement shall have been accomplished? Fancy a man in England requiring to go to British Guiana, and in order to get there, must first proceed to Jamaica ! x We may, however, be told that as a foreign possession we have nothing to do with such a question, and in this view of the case we shall he prudent, and say nothing. We acknowledge ourselves indebted to the U. M. S. P. Company for the patronage they bestow upon 11s, and our voice will be loud in maintaining for them facilities and advantages here, compatible with the importance and magnitude of the service. But in jdain and unvarnished truth, do the Jamaicans believe that it is from an especial desire to serve and bestow favors on St. Thomas, that the Company have selected it as a rendezvous for their ships ? or is it that they are sensible of our Island being an extremely convenient port to them? We are not in a hutnour to be boastful, but let us ask, may not St. Thomas, with its immense connexions, afford the steam-ships arriving here some business ? If we are answered in the negative, then say we, let the Company establish Jamaica as head quarters, and a formidable competitor to their business will present itself very soon. Ci naku's line, altho' not yet in the fore-ground, has not omitted to include St. Thomas in its routes. In the summer we are to have a steamer from that enterprising Com-

pany, capable of conveying one hundred passengers þÿ New York is an agreeable detour for passengers going to Europe. Our own merchants are about to provide an efficient steamer to form a line between St. Jago deCuba, Santo Domingo, Curasao, Porto Rico, and St. Thomas. If we bad a true confession, it would be an acknowledgement that it is from the Jbreign ports in the West Indies that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company derive their gains, and not from the British colonies þÿ and St. Thomas has a prcponderenee over all these together. A word more before we conclude. Do the Jamaicans not know that St. Thomas flourished, and was money-making, long

before the Royal Mail Steam service came into existence? Can the Jamaicans suppose that the British steam-ships coming to this port is the nucleus of our prosperity? Do they believe that the Port-Royal or Kingston becoming by rendezvous of the R. 31. Steamers, their commerce would increase so immeasurably as to spread wealth throughout the lanil ? We entertain a contrary opinion ; we believe Jamaica's prosperity lies in her fertile fields ; let them be meliorated as in days of yore þÿ let her cultivate sugar-cane, coffee, cocoa, cotton, indigo, cochineal, all indegenous to her soil þÿ let her sea-hoard be filled with warehouses containing an abundance of those tropical products þÿ let her, in order to achieve these, be more practical and less theoretical, and the patronaffe of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company will to her he a matter of small account þÿ and above all, let her leave us alone. þÿ Editor Tidenue.

Never had a man entrusted with high uithority so noble a chance as that which was offered to the President of the French Republic on the first day of the present year. lie had summarily destroyed a Constitution which had the fatal demerit of being unworkable ; lie bad appealed to the people ratify to Ins violent act, and to grant him fresh powers for the government of the country ; and the people had answered his appeal by a majority, possibly exaggerated, but most undoubtedly triumphant and decisive. Up to that period, though 'here was much to condemn in his conduct, there was also much to he said in extenuation, or, at all events, in explanation, o) it. Rut Ins success, so much greater than lie anticipated, appeals to have turned his head; and every individual act, and the whole aggregate of his acts, between the first day ol the

» <e m © a x A 'T u a year and the period at which we write, has not only been a mistake as regards his own position, but a crime against his country and against the public and private morality of all Europe. History offers no example of such prodigious and wanton tyranny as he has exhibited, of such gratuitous cruelty and wrong, or of such suicidal and parricidal outrage þÿ suicidal as regards his own prospects, and parricidal as regards the interesls and liberties of that generous and unfortunate nation to whom he owes everything. The wholesale deportations to Cayenne ; the banishment of many of the most illustrious of living Frenchmen without trial, and without even the allegation of a crime or an offence ; the utter annihilation of all freedom of speech, writing, and action; and the etablishnient of a grinding, unconscionable, and bloodthirsty despotism, successively astonished and alarmed Europe; and tor all these acts he found, unfortunately, that the men by whose aid he effected his coup d'etat were, if not ready and zealous, at all events obedient instruments. Rut there was a point to he reached in his career to which not even these men could consent to follow or to he dragged after him. M. de Morny, who served him so effectually in December, discovered bis own conscience in January, and, much to his credit, refused to sign the decree lor the confiscation of the property of the Orleans family. Even M. Dupin, whose politics were of the colour of the religion of the famous Vicar of Bray, and

chielly consisted in maintaining his own position at the Cour de Cassation, whatever might be the Government, and whomsoever might be the ruler of France, could not reconcile it to his honour, his dignity, or his self-respect to hold a judicial office under a tyrant who outraged justice and common honesty in so glaring a manner. In a remarkable and very spirited letter, which the newspapers of Paris have not been permitted to publish, hut which lias been given to the world by the journals of London and Brussels, that eminent functionary has administered a rebuke which the French President, callous as lie appears to be, must acutely feel, and for which it is probable that M. Dupin may, some fine morning, find himself an exile in Leices- , ter-square, or, worse still, in the pestilential swamps of Cayenne. Rut such breathless races as Louis Napoleon is Ministry, consisting of: Jifahmc as moral sense of mankind can never be vernntent. running are of necessity short ones. The outraged with impunity. It was not so much the misgovernment of Louis Philippe, or the ungovernableness of the French people, that caused the revolution ot February, 1848, as the public disgust at the meanness of his conduct towards the unhappy Queen ol Spain. It was the Spanish marriages which «» " rendered all hands powerless to preserve his throne, and which deprived him of the courage to strike a blow for the maintenance of his authority. The Orleans tainily would, in all human probability, have still been on the throne of

France, if it had not been for the disgraceful intrigues which transformed the l)uc de Moutpensier into a Spanish prince, and gave his children a claim to the crown of Spain. Louis Napoleon, in confiscating or endeavouring to confiscate the property of the Orleans family, has committed an act still meaner fore, not effected than that was, and sooner or later he will meet his reward for it. There is a moral grandeur in public, opinion, and in the public sentiment of what is light and generous, which no man, however exalted, and however powerful, can brave probably with impunity. Louis Napoleon is, even now, almost isolated ; lie lias no friends except among the needy, the desperate, and the profligate ; and what their friendship is worth þÿ if it be not a desecration

ol the name to apply it to the feelings of such people þÿ the records of all human experience abundantly prove. At the first symptom of a change for the worstin his fortunes, the whole crew will desert him, and those who now eat the crumbs from his table will, we may he sure, he the first under such circumstan ces to consign him to the swamps where he has sent so many of his countrymen, or to expedite a sharper and more fatal catastrophe. That a man who for upwards of three years played so prudent a part, and who in difficulty and adversity appeared to show heart as well as head, should in the days of his prosperity exhibit so lamentable a want of both, is the most extraordinary incident of our " Querr. Dens vult times. The old and trite proverb, penlere. prius demen tat," has received a new exemplification ; and all Europe repeats it at each new freak of tyranny on the part of the President. and expects at no distant day the inevitable con summation. þÿ -

,V. Thomas Times, 10/// March 1852. Fire at SI. SlarSliohmicH ! The town of Gustavia, in the Island of St. Bartholomew, lias been visited hv a very severe conflagration. The fire, we learn, broke out on Tuesday morning, (tile 2nd instant), at 2 þÿo clock in that part of the Town known as the 3rd and most populous section, reducing to ashes, it is supposed, no fewer than two hundred houses. The flames increased and spread so rapidly that it became totally impossible for any of the inhabitants to remove any portion of moveable property from the burning district, and with very few exceptions even wearing apparel could not be ( saved, hut was left to feed the consuming elements. The fire raged with unfury the whole of Tuesday, dur- j ing which time all efforts made to suppress its progress proved unavailing. The Island had been suffering before the lire from a long drought, which caused the houses, mostly old, to lie considerably more iutiaminahle, and when it is remembered that that Island possesses few or no tanks for the collecting and supplying of water, it may easily he seen how incapable must have been the inhabitants to arrest the progress of the Haines. From the letters received here, and which we have been allowed to peruse, it is clear that many of the population who may have been of much service in saving wearing apparel and other articles Irom the dwellings prior to their being destroyed by the lire, became so alarmed and panic struck that they Your splendid, unexpected, and mi- I sought refuge on hoard the vessels

lying in port, where they remained until the lire subsided. That portion of the present a most awl ul spectacle, as nothing remains to he seen, hut wall foundations, kitchens and chimneys, burning cinders, dead dogs, hogs, goats, cats, poultry, <fcc. One aged female is said to have lost her life, hut under what circumstances we have not heard. Immediately after the distressing news reached the island of St. Martins, a hurried subscription, we learn, was there got up, and with the proceeds, articles of food, <fco., were obtained and despatched for the temporary rciiefofthe sufferers. A subscription list was also pen and the tongue of him w ho desires | here set on foot yesterday and promises | to be crowned with much success. Would it not he a prudent and becoming act, on the part of those interested with the subscription list in this island, if a cargo of lumber were sent at once to St. Barths, in order that small huts could he erected, as temporary shelters for those who otherwise would have to continue on hoard or possibly sleep in the open heavens V

Those who have witnessed a fire in St. Thomas, know that such measures have at suck times been resorted to. A singular circumstance is related to have occurred connected with the fire: þÿ A young female who had for many years been suffering from insanity, suddenly became restored to her sane mind, and now continues in the full possession of her faculties, and has since taken her share with the other members of her family in prosecuting any work or business to lie done.

ANNEXATION OF BELGIUM. The Duke of Bassano, the new French envoy to Hie court of Belgium, arrived at Brussels on Thursday last. One ol the demands which M. de Bassano is charged to make from the Belgian Government is the removal of the monumental lion þÿI rontthe field of Waterloo, and the demolition of the pyramidal mound of triumph which it crowns. Soon after the revolution of July the destruction of the same trophy was talked of as a point insisted on by the Government of Louis Philippe, and when tlit French expedition returned from the siege of Antwerp, in passing over tinplain of Waterloo, it was expected that they would have taken the law into their own hands, and hurled the offensive symbol of \ ic tot ions force from his proud eminence. But they were dissuaded from this violent project hy an ofl'et r. who suggested that it would he much easier to stamp the tropl y with ridicule than to overturn it. Therefore, he proposed that they should knock out the þÿlion s teeth, and pare his claws. This practical sarcasm was unanimously approved, and the expressive mutilation forthwith carried into effect. The application now made hy Louis Naj o i< i tortile demolition of llu trophy makes one recall his laconic declaration la lore the Court of Peers, when tried lor l it < seditious attempt at Boulogne, lie then said: þÿ þÿ represent I as principle tl < sovereignly of the people, as svsttm the empire, and as action the retrieval ot þÿWaterloo. The two first points have

been carried, and it is certain that no means will be neglected to ucliicvi tinlast. It is a þÿ fixed þÿidea with the President, and all may rest assured that lie will prosecute it with the dogged tenacity of purpose which marks his character. Meanwhile it is true that the prince ridicules the preparations for national defence against invasion which are talked of in England; and it is said he mentioned, the other day, at his dinner table, as an instance of the crotchets which prevailed in some heads across the Channel on this subject, that an English gentle man had shown hint a plan which lie had foimcd for the fortification of his own mansion as a precaution against piratical incursions of the French in case of war. But nothing would lie less conclusive than to infer the pacific intentions of Louis Napoleon from such ridicule ; since it is well known that lie treated with disdainful mockery 1he surmises ot a coup d'etat at the moment when the project which has scornfully disavowed was matured in his head, and lie was only waiting for an apt juncture to strike the long meditated blow. The fall ot Lord Palmerston, however, having forced the President of the Republic to abandon the summary mode of annexing Belgium to France which he had at first contemplated, hy means of a simple decree inserted in the Mouitcur , and being now forced to adopt the more slow hut equally sure mode of attaining the same object, hy means of first sap pine the allegiance of lint people P

their Sovereign, and then takin" posses- .sion of the country under pretence that the offer of annexation came front 15 elgium itself, Louis Napoleon turns his leisure moment to a change of policy towards Switzerland a country þÿ which offers him great attractions, as he hopes to make it the means of a coalition between himself and Austria against Lnghtnd. The Swiss journals mention that the Government of the Republic is in a state of great alarm, on account ot a new note which has been sent to it hy the French Government. As far as I can learn, the French Government not only insists on the expulsion of all the French refugees who are suspected ot country for to that demand the plotting þÿ against the Government ol Swiss their Government at once, and without the slightest hesitation, gave its consent þÿ but it insists on the Swiss Government closing all clubs, and on its employing energetic measures against any popular manifestations which have been got up in that country for the purpose of forcing the Government to have new elections. Meanwhile a rumour is current which has reference to the state of feeling in certain districts of Belgium, as also of some regiments of t he Belgian army. It this rumour can he depended on, it would imply that a feeling unfavourable to their own Government, and too favourable to France, is apparent. There is, however, reason to believe that something not of an ordinary nature is going on with respect to the relations of France u ith Germany and the powers generally ;
and it may be that the quasi decree on the subject, circulated privately, is, after all, a serious fact.

It contains a series of desatches from Sir C. A. Fitzroy to Earl Grey, enclosing the reports which had been made to him by the Inspector of Crown l/inds, the Geological Surveyor, and by other persons, with reference to the discovery of gold at Bathurst, and other parts of Australia. Sir Charles þÿI itzrov gives a narrative of events preceding and leading to the establishment if the fact of the colony containing gold fields, and reports that up to the 19th ot' Vugust, 1851, gold to the value of CTO, IKK! had been shipped from Sydney. The value of the gold discovered hy humid and dry assay appears to be £\ ISs. 4d. per ounce. The specimens submitted to the Colonial Government were extremely fine, and appeared to be exactly identical in I)r. m California. quality Iverr, of Wallawa, to that found has lodged in the Union Bank of Australia the largest piece of gold which has vet been discovered in any part of the world. The total weight of this block was lOGIb. and, after deducting portions for samples, the net weight deposited in ihe bank was 102lb. 9oz., and 5dwts. The finding of the auriferous block is thus described : þÿ þÿ A few days ago, an educated aboriginal, formerly attached to the Wellington Mission, and who has been in the service of W. J. Kerr, Esq., of Wallawa, about seven years, returned home to his

employer with the intelligence that he had discovered a large mass of gold amongst a heap of quartz, upon the run whilst tending his sheep. Gold being the universal topic of conversation, the curiosity of this sable son of the forest was excited, and provided with a tomahawk he had amused himself by exploring the country adjacent to his þÿemployer s l and, and had thus made the discovery. 1 1 is attention was first called to the lucky spot by observing speck a

© U E> It a ATI s« of some glittering yellow subs ance upon tbe surface of a block of tie quart/., upon which he applied his tomahawk, and broke off a portion. At tint moment the splendid prize stood revelled to his 1 sight. 1 1 is first care was to start off home and disclose his discovery to his master, to whom he presented whatever gold might be procured fron it. As may be supposed, little time vas lost by the worthy doctor. Quick ashorseflesh would carry him he was on tie ground, and in a very short period the three blocks of quartz, containing tin hundredweight of gold, were released from the bed where, charged with unknown wealth, they had rested perhaps for thousands of years, awaiting the hand of civilised man to disturb them. The largest of the blocks was about a foot in diameter, and weighed 751b. gross. Out oft his piece GOIb. of pure gold was taken. Before separation it was beautifully encased in quartz. The other two were something smaller. The auriferous mass weighed, as nearly as could be guessed, from two to three cut. Not being able to move it conveniently, Dr. Kerr broke the pieces into small fragments, and herein committed a very grand error. As specimens the glittering blocks would have been invaluable. Nothing yet known of would have borne comparison, or, if any, the comparison would have been in our favour. From the description given by him, as seen in their original like them state, the world has seen nothing j yet. þÿ The heaviest of the two last pieces presented an appearance not unlike a

honeycomb or sponge, and consisted of particles of a crystalline form, as did nearly the whole of the gold. The second large piece was smoother, and the particles more condensed, and seemed as if it had been acted upon hy w ater. The remainder was broken into lumps of from tw o to three pounds, and dow nwards, and were remarkably free from quartz or earthly matter; when heaped together on the table they presented a splendid appearance, and shone with an effulgence calculated to dazzle the brain of any man not armed with the coldness of stoicism. þÿ The spot where this mass of treasure was found will be celebrated in the golden annals of these districts, and we as our means of information will allow shall, therefore, describe it as minutely . In the first place, the quartz blocks formed an isolated heap, and were distant about 100 yards from a quartz vein which stretches up the ridge from the Murroo Creek. The locality is the commencement of an undulating table land, very fertile, and is contiguous to a neverfailing supply of water in the abovenamed creek. It is distant about 54 miles from Bathurst, 18 from Mudgee, 30 from Wellington, and 18 to the nearest point of the Macquarie River, and is within eight miles of Dr. þÿKerr shead station. His þÿMajesty Letter s Patent, to the inhabitants of llis Westindia Islands, dated Kith of June 1851, will, þÿ ofa truth, become a royal evidence of favor and solicitude for the true welfare of the þÿpopulation. By doing, however, so we have come to enter on various matters not treated of in the present Project, but which we conceive ought to be consideredjf a new Law is to lie framed, and we have believed that we ought so much the less to abstain even where our observations only contain hints and allusions as this, even in case the change only is entered on, which we consider as a necessity, that, namely, of introducing two Colonial Councils, one lor St. Croix, and one i >r St. Thomas and St Johns, which are solely to be assembled together, for questions in common, whereby it cannot l>e avoided hearing the opinions of the inhabitants through their deputies. In respect to their election, we must, according to the nature and importance of law, advise, that it be done in the manner which we, in conformity to the present project have pointed out below. But, if the Project, however, is to go back, other changes and additions might also be admitted if found appropriate. Willi these in mind we pass on to the contents of the various paragraphs. H 1-3. The Committee must approve that the business of the Colonial-Council be limited to counseling or advising, and must accede to what has been stated on the head by the 10 Men in their report; (Appendix No. 30 column 457) ; also, to

what was said by the Minister of Finance when he laid the Project before the Diet. (Lundsthingstidcnde, column 327.) On tins head we must finally refer to what we shall state below of the likely constituency and powers of the Colonial- Council, and then only say besides, that legislation about communes ; public roads; trades, and the like, easily give occasion to party-strife, especially where political acquirements and discretion, can lie taken for granted, as but little, and parties will not readily yield to a local decision, only of the Colonial- Council and Governor. It cannot, there-

3 5K CS«n A'rgS. fore, hurt, if Forms of Legislation, in the beginning at least, until parliamentary tact is developed, be of such a kind as may prevent hasty measures. 2 Let: b. makes over the legislative power in respect to local ordinances, to the King under the responsibility of the respective Minister, and we cannot otherwise than be sensible that preponderating reasons plead for vesting this authority in the hands of the monarch. But when Let : v,. likewise, makes over to the king, under the like responsibility, the issuing of Ordinances, which subsequently, under a certain eventuality must be laid before the Diet, this might give occasions of collisions between the Legislative-Powers, which ought to be prevented. In this respect it should ever be borne in mind, that the Fundamental-Law only distinguishes betwixt laws issued in the usual manner, and those issued provisionally, and that it does not name a third kind. The title þÿ þÿOrdinances, cannot thus change the relation, which conformable to the Constitution or Fundamental-Law shall exist between the Monarch and the Diet, in respect to the legislative power, pursuant to which no full valid law can be given by the monarch alone, and a Provisional One falls to the ground when not sanctioned by the Diet. Now when it is subsequently said in the Paragraph: þÿ Whenever these ordinances contain deviations, these, as well as the opinions of the Colonial-Council must be laid before the Diet at the earliest meeting. Should no gainsaying

arise, or the objections that are made, do not cause any alteration therein, the ordinance stands þÿenforced: it thence follows !>t, That ordinances already issued by the king are subject to the criticism and scrutiny of tiie Diet, which beyond a case of necessity ought rather to be avoided, and 2, ir/iat is still more dangerous, that such ordinances against which the Diet has raised objections, may still be enforced, as, in accordance to the royal Veto, these objections need not be heeded. This will not at all do, and, therefore, there is nothing else to be done, than frankly, under the respective þÿMinister s legal responsibility, also, to vest the legislative power in the king respecting those ordinances stated in 1 Let: a., or to place them under the regulation $ 3. We would side for, that it would be more to the purpose to choose the lirst alternative, about which we will subsequently take the liberty of referring, whilst we will here only observe that when the controling power reserved by the Diet is sufficient in respect to those laws that concern local matters named sub Let: n., it also appears that it might be left to Government, under the same control, to decide about, and how far those laws passed for Denmark, harmonise with Colonial Relations. tion of the Fundamental-Law; as a Law for the Colonies would straightway carry along with it the same political rights for the inhabitants there, as for the inhubitantsof the Mother-Country, whence would ensue the Colonies participation in legislative powers by self-elected representatives, according to the law of election prevalent here. But in those discussions which preceded the issuing of the Fundamental-Law, it is advanced, that it was not contemplated to be made valid in the Colonies, and when it is considered, that the greater part of the population there have attained civil rights only a few years ago; that many of the

inhabitants of the Colonies possess but very little mental developement : and finally, that the population is composed of divers nations, among which the Danish constituency and interest for the institutions of the Mother Country are least prominent i it cannot then be considered advisable to establish an institution which in the Colony, would become a source ot ferment and party-strife, and the result whereof, only some tew representatives meeting in the Diet, might be of doubtful signilicancy, as their votes of course would only plead a special interest. Besides which, it would scarcely prove beneficial to the Colonies that, all legislative acts which concern them should be transacted in the Diet; the major part of the members being unacquainted with Colonial relations, and, thus, must either vote laws blindly, or else demand such a number of elucidations, that business will progress very slowly, and take up a disproportionate part of the þÿDiet time. s To be continued.'

We have received New York papers to the 8th instant; but from want of room, are compelled to defer our extracts for our next number. The principal items ire as follows : The resignation of the Russell ministry, and the formation ot a new cabinet þÿ the Earl of Derby, First Lord of the Treasury and Prime Minister. It was rumoured that the British squadron, which will consist of twelve to fifteen line of battle ships, a similar number of frigates, corvettes and sloops, and about ten of the finest war-steamers, will be kept cruising in the English channel. Accounts from Lisbon state that the Portuguese were preparing for all contingencies and for the eventualities of a European war. The Belgian Government has ordered an augmentation of 100 men in each of the battalions of the regiments. Several of the Swiss journals report to the effect that the Federal Council had demanded the intervention ofGreat Britain against France, and that the French Minister was preparing to depart. The number of arrests in France had amounted to 100,000.

DISTRESSING SITUATION OF TI1E SUFFERERS. Appeal lo the Community of St. Croix.

On Tuesday the 2nd Inst: a large portion of the Town of Gustavia was destroyed by a conflagration whose fury in the outset baffled all the elforts made to subdue its fearful progress. 'I'he Fire commenced at 2 þÿo clock in the morning and spread with such fearful rapidity, that the morning Sun rose over the smoking ruins of 200 HOUSES, and A BEGGARED PEOPLE!! the inmates driven by the flames fled, abandoning their all and were compelled to hurry to the beach, where numbers were taken on board the Vessels in Port. By this awful visitation, the People of a Colony within a few miles from our shores have been reduced to misery it not despair. Respectable Families, Mothers, Widows, or Orphans are involved in one common ruin, the rich and poor have been equally crushed. On the announcement of the calamity, an appeal was made to the Inhabitants of St. Thomas; the voice of sympathy responded to that appeal, and the sum of $1000 subscribed within three days has been placed into my hands as evidence, that the sorrow generally expressed is not confined to barren words. I nder these painful circumstances there is every reason to anticipate, that the sentiments ot pity, and commisseration alluded to, are not only confined to this Island, hut also extends to a Sister Colony whose inhabitants arc known to he equally zealous, in the works of charity and benevolence, and that this appeal in behalf of the unfortunates will not be made in vain. St. Thomas, 15th March 1852. JOSEPH de GOUT.
