matters, and that the same will partly he the case with the Governors who are sent out from time to time, so that they, for a while, at least, may get ensnared in their views, it is alas! not of doubtful imagining that, Colonial legislation may he developed in a less fortunate bias. But under the inconveniencies that will exist whether the one or the other is chosen, it is yet more probable that, the special interest and affairs of the Colo nies will he more attended to by the Minister whose occupation places him in constant communication with the Co Ionics, than it will he by the Diet ; and also, that any public discussion that might take place would scarcely obtaii a majority, when the responsible Minis ter sided in an opposite direction. A long string of abuses, could not, undo existing circumstances, pass unnoticed by the Diet, that can demand explana tions and call the Minister to account, in regard to anything which concerns tin Colonies, and thus, they will come with in the sphere of the Diet, and enjoy benefits from the institutions of tin Mother-Country, though the Constitution of the Mother-Country he not ii full force in the Colonies. Although we thus deem, that the so called active civic lights should not, at present, be granted to the Colonies, there still remains one question þÿ whether a part of those regulations treated of n that part of the Fundamental law which concern personal rights and the rights of property might not he made applicable in the Colonies? This question tin

Committee believe they must answer þÿat firmatively. As to what concerns the press, wt must not omit mentioning, that lor a lenght ot time representations were sen' in io the Government then existing, ir respect to its being freed in analogy to the times. It may certainly lie deemed unnecessary here to explain those ad vantages a free press would produce ii. the Colonies, amongst which, it will no' he the least, that a knowledge of tin state of things, and what agitates tin public mind there, will soonest and most surely reach the Mother Country, and that a firmer union between if and th< Colonies, by the immediate and speediei communication will thus ensue. Neither must it he overlooked that the large ma jority of the educated classes in the Co lonies have gone there from countries which stand high m political intelligence, and that they keep up a constant communication with them, so that opposing such a measure would be doubly felt by them ; we must also add that the productions of an unshackled press are of most general perusal, as the English pa pers are read by all and every one. On the other hand, it ought not to pass unnoticed, that the liberty of the press is not devoid of scruples. Two newspapers, only, are printed on the is lands, each of which is issued hut twice a week, as advertising and political in telligencers and, that in respect tothelat ter they have obtained licences under tlu supervision of the respective Police Ma gistrates. These newspapers take theii

articles partly from those issued in the English colonies, and partly from those issued in England and America, not only as concernsforeign countries, but also as regards Denmark. The last circumstanc evinces a most lamentable ignorance among the respective Editors, with tlu danish tongue and with danish affairs, and therein lies one of those essential scruples above alluded to. Besides this, a free press orders itself quite different it a small than in a large community, and it might he feared that, a newspaper dc void of restrictions, in the hands of; publisher who would agree to work foi such payment as the owner of the pros? might offer, would not unfrequontly b«

employed in injurious attacks on private character. It might however he possible that these scruples could he removed, as when the Danish law of the press is presented for extension to the Colonies, the Colonial Council might he aide to cause such a regulation as may afford some security that each respective and responsible publisher do possess such personal qualities as may afford security against the annoyances above mentioned. If we now pass on to the organization of the Colonial Council , we at once come to the consideration that the relations in our islands do not range themselves as in the British and the French Colonies, where natives and Europeans are knit together by language, manners, religion &.C., and where they exactly know and follow every thing that takes place in the Mother Country; but, our Danish element in the community consist of officials from whom the greater part of the native population are divided by language and manners, which is also the case with the numerous and influential foreigners who reside in the islands. A communal tie naturally exists, but the tie that should entwine and unite the islands, generally; that homogenial nationality is wanting, to which is yet to he added, that the principal islands are as essentially different, as the chief occupation of the þÿinhabitants agriculture and commerce. The elements of a representative body, that ought not essentially to consist of Danish office holders, are, therefore, not at hand, and the Council

might, in consequence, very easily, be ruled by only a few who possess those acquirements which from the heterogeneous population, and deficiency of education among the natives, is not generally found. It must not he overlooked that for this population, little has hitherto been done, through schools, to educate them as Danish citizens, and that in future it will he exceedingly difficult to do the needfu . It is also an act ot great injustice, to the storekeeper, who fears his Cod and respects both the law and its spirit ; who desires to see the humble and the ignorant elevated in the social scale, to have this advantage taken of him by those who fear not Cod, neither regard the voice ot man. II the Lutheran Church is open even for a holiday, the police compel an orderly quiet. But the members ol the English Church, they who contribute such a heavy item to the taxes of the Island, they whose number and respectability cannot ho questioned, have had the sanctity of their Sabbath broken by the unholy stiver hunters of the market, hitherto without redress. I am, Sir, Your obedient servant, A It est- Under. March 23d, 1852.

The most important subject of a local nature we have to deal with for the week is the grounding on the shoal ot "little Saba" of Cu.n ahd's screw propellor Merlin , which occurred at eleven o'clock on Wednesday night (the 17th.) After much exertion on the part of Capt. Cope and crew, she was got off' by one o'clock on the following morning, having been fast for about two hours; the force with which she struck when she grounded appears to have been so severe that the shaft which governs the screw broke, and the consequence was that she could not with her machinery make this port. The night was extremely calm, which prevented her sails being ol use, so that she continued drifting to leeward. In this dilemma, the Captain dispatched a boat with six men lor this place, to give information of the accident that had befallen him. The boat arrived here at live o'clock on Thursday morning, having rowed a distance of about eight miles. Immediately on the intelligence becoming known to the Harbour Master, and the Merlin's Agent, Mr. Swift, those gentlemen of the barges unitedly succeeded to obtain the Danish ships Christian and Jeanclfe, manned each with tour hands and the Captain, who at once proceeded to the Merlin; about noon the Captain of the Christian brought to the King's Wharf some of the steamer's passengers and luggage. These boats, however, were unable to render any service in the wn\ of bringing her into port ; and she would consequently have continued to drift to leeward until, may

be, she would have had the good luck to make some anchoring giound along the coast of Porto Hieo. However, as fortune would have it, the French warsteamer Crocodile, Captain Ciloux, made our port about 1 1 o'clock a. m., on Thursday, and the French Consul, M. PiccioM, directly sent a note to her commander apprising him of a distressed English steamer being to leeward unable to make her way up, and requesting of him, if no special service prevented, to render her whatever service it was in his power to afford. The request, we are truly happv to state, was with every promptitude

complied with, and Captain K.i/t".u, who had, as Deputy Port Captain, gone out to meet the Crocodile , accompanied her down, to facilitate her movements about the small Islands and quays to the Westward of us. The Crocodile met the Merlin about 4 miles to leeward of where she had struck, unable to render herselt any help. Hawsers from the French steamer were payed out to the Merlin, and in a few minutes she was safely in tow. At two o'clock both came into port. ( Conl i lined from \o. 851). ) The Fundamental outlines of the regulation here proposed will therefore be these : " For the West-India Possessions, there be instituted two Colonial-Councils, one for St. Croix, and one for St. Thomas and St. Johns, which possess consultative co-operation in the exercise of legislative power." " These Colonial-Councils, likewise, talce over, separately, the independent Government of Communal-Alfairs instead of the Burgher-Councils hitherto existing; the one for St. Croix, the other for St. Thomas and St. Johns under supervision of Government." " The Governor, every year, summons the Colonial-Councils to a joint meeting, to diseuss the Westindiu Budget and Chief Account together with such other matters of special importance for the islands, collectively, as the Governor may lay before them for discussion." " Fach Colonial-Council to consist of Members elected by the inhabitants, and of 'J Members nominated by the king; the election of Members to be according to the prescripts contained in the Colonial-Law." In the Project laid before us there is one regulation wanting: of the application of I lie lien lines mid of the I )isbu esculents oj the II est india Possessions to the mints of the Colonics ; a regulation which we in adherence to our preceding expressions, are of opinion ought to be embodied in the law. We consider it, namely, as not impossible, and at all events, as a Gaol, that we should strive to reach, that the Mother-Countrv be freed

from any direct contribution towards the expenses of the Colonies, nay ! that it even might be attainable, that the Colony eventually bound itself to pay a certain annual contribution to the Finances. It might, perhaps appear rigid to make such a claim so speedily after the revolution which has occurred in the Colonics, but as we in a re-organization, in the Colonies, themselves, of their revenues and disbursements, behold the only real means of preserving them for i lie Mother-Country, which, especially as matters now stand, appears desirable from more than one point of view, we could not avoid mentioning the matter. ITere is however, a subject of the greatest importance connected with this which will require considerable preliminary work : a settlement of the relation between The Koyal Colonial Treasury and The Land Treasuries. On each of the English islands exist, a local Island Treasury, which is entirely under the supervision id' the Colonial-Council, and which with few exceptions, defrays both the Commercial and the Colonial or State Disbursements, such as: The Administration; Courts of Justice; the Clergy; Legislative Assembly ; the Military; þÿ in part þÿ The Militia; Roads or Highways A.e. Ac. When it be lirstlixed or settled what contribution is to be paid to the Mother-Country, there might without apprehension be given to the Colonies an essential influence on the Colonial Budget, and it certainly should be borne hi mind that the wcitare ot the Colonies can just as well be

affected by the imposition of disproportionate Communal-burdens (if such, from the rigid separation between the Communal Treasury, and the Royal Colonial Treasury, might become necessary), as it could be by disproportionately increas-

a ?i\ 0 li 0 It ing the lloyal Taxes and Imposts. On the whole, it interests the inhabitants of the Colony, in the highest degree, to know, that the amounts of the direct atnl indirect imposts are applied in a correct and appropriate manner, þÿ a knowledge which in times past, to the injury olthe Mother-Country, has been wanting. What has hitherto stood in the way ot the so called Land-Treasuries being incorporated with the Royal Treasury is the relation wherein the Colonies stand at present to the Mother-Country in financial respects, namely, in as far as it is feared that a union as the one above mentioned, which local relations and the small size ot the Colonies render desirable, would occasion the revenues to be appropriated less, than at present, to the benefit of the islands. If the obstacle above alluded to be removed, at all events so, that it be imposed on the Colonies to yield the Mother-Country only a certain annua! contribution, then a union of the Land-Treasuries and the Royal Colonial Treasury might be thought of in this way: That a joint treasure lie established for St. ( 'roi.e and one also for St. Thomas anil St. Johns. On the other hand it is not feasible to unite all the Landtreasuries, to a mutual or joint Communal Treasury, as St. Croix and St. Thomas, as precedingly explained, have different interests entirely ; here is Commerce, there Agriculture; the town in one, the Country in the other is of preponderating importance. Such a union, which is necessary because, as

has been mentioned, there cannot be drawn anv determinate boundary between what concerns the State, and what concerns the Commune, in small and distant Colonies, would cause the possibility of introducing order into the accounts, so that the system of taxation could be firmly based, and enable Government to get an insight into Colonial Finances ; not to mention, that administrative disbursements would thereby be spared. In conformity herewith, and what is otherwise elucidated above, it is furthermore proposed, that the following regulations lie embodied, in suitable places, in the Colonial-Law: "In the Danish Westindia Possessions, the Executive power is intrusted to the Governor appointed by the king, under the superior guidance of the respective Minister." " The adjudicative I'ower lies with the Courts, solely to be governed by Law." " The king appoints to office, and can dismiss and remove functionaries, in conformity to the Fundamental-Law. Their pensions are to lie fixed in accordance to the Colonial Pension Law." " Danish Law and Justice are furthermore to prevail in the Colonies." " Ad tax can be imposed, changed, or abrogated, " All disbursements for the Colonies, except by law." under which is included those for the army and navy, according to approximate regulations, are to be liquidated from the taxes and customs raised in the Colonies. When a balance is brought to pass in the Colonial Head Account, it shall by law be settled what contribution is to be yielded to the State Treasury."

"The chief Colonial Accounts are to be revised by arrangements of the Colonial-Council ; the final decision lies with the Minister of Finance." In respect to those rights which the Fundamental Law secures to Danish Citizens, regarding persons and property, those, however, excepted, which arC treated of in the aforesaid law's 4th and 5th divisions, it must be considered, prior to the issuing of the Colonial Law , which of these right? may lie awarded the inhabitants of the Colonies, according to the peculiar relations of the place, and what regulations in this respect should be admitted in the Colonial-Law

The new Cholera and Fever Bill, which abolishes the absurd and injurious quarantine system in Denmark, has passed the Upper House by a majority of 12 to 4. The Marine Minister has asked a grant for the equipment of the screw-steamer Tlior, and a three months' expedition of the same, to try its qualities. ITALY. Rome, Feb. 20. þÿ Yesterday morning þÿ the Roman sbirri made a grand discovery, no less than a whole shopfull of daggers, crackers, small shells, and other infernal machines, with which it is supposed the Corso would have been strewed by the Red Republicans. It is said that a list of some 40 persons, especially destined for attack, iias been discovered. Yesterday and last night numerous arrests were made. The exact number of persons implicated is not yet known. The police does not scruple to put its hands on whomsoever falls under the suspicion of the authorities; and the consequence is, that, in its zeal for maintaining order, it frequently occurs that persons are taken up who are not connected with the anti-papal leaguers. It is said that upwards of 50 were taken from their homes. The Opinione quotes a letter from Milan of the 25th ult., stating that the police had received orders to exercise the strictest surveillance over English travellers. It is with great difficulty the latter can obtain passports, and, with rare exceptions, they are not to be permitted to sojourn more than twenty-four hours in Lombardy. The Genoa Gazette publishes the following account of the disorders which took place at Sassari on the 24th ult.; þÿ "Some civilians cainc to blows in an inn with a party of soldiers of the rifle corps. Their cries drew to the scene of the riot a crowd of other individuals, both civil and military, and a general collision ensued. The town was thrown
into the greatest confusion ; the drums beat to arms, and the national guard

turned out. The intendant sent to the spot a detachment of light horse, on which the national guard tired, killing the sergeant in command and a rifleman. The troops returned the fire, and, in the melee, there were some killed and wounded on both sides." The latest accounts announce that tranquility has been completely restored.

New Mode of Operating in Surgery. þÿ it is known to the professors of natural philosophy that a platina wire can be heated instantaneously to a red beat, by means of a powerful electric battery þÿ þÿ and that in that state it will cut through the skin and flesh of the human body with more ease than the sharpest instrument. The surgeons of the Santa Theresa Hospital, in Vienna, have made the experiment of substituting such a wire for the usual surgical instruments in some of their operations; and it is said with perfect success. They have laid a I memoir on the subject before the imperial Academy of Science in that capital. Important Discovery for Seamen. þÿ Mr. Thompson, surgeon, II. N., the inventor of the naval telegraphic lights, has submitted a plan to the lords commissioners of the admiralty by which candles and oil may for ever he dispensed with, many thousands of pounds annually being saved to the country, and yet t .mi times more light secured to every ship afloat ; this is accomplished by a simple and a very ingenious method ot using the slush from salt meats, now of no use. Their lordships have approved ol the invention ; and since the order was given by the admiralty, her Majesty's ship Impregnable, flag-ship, Devonport, has been lighted from stem to stern on this new plan. The men in each ship, tn place of having one dip of 3-4 to the pound, have now a light for six hours equal to 16 dips, and from which, by the aid of a parabolic reflector, they are en-

abled to read 30 feet oil". This candletube may be filled with water, yet it can be instantly expelled, and the light fully maintained. The grease is so locked up that it cannot well escape, so that the lamp may be rolled about the deck. Dangersof Paris. The Blessed Sashes! þÿ A letter from Madrid, dated the 4th instant says : þÿ " Yesterday the solemn ceremony of the presentation of the blessed sashes which the Pope has sent tor the young princess took place at the Royal Palace. The Papal Nuncio at Madrid, Monsignor Brunelli, Archbishop of Thessalonica, was the person charged with the presentation. lie was conducted with great pomp from his own palace to that of the Queen in the midst of a large assembly of people. On Ins arrival at the palace gates, he was escorted by the halberdiers, with their hand of music, up the grand staircase. On being introduced into the royal presence he made a speech full of compliments to the noble, glorious, and heroical Spanish nation, and the successors of St. Ferdinand. The Nuncio then presented the brief to her Majesty, who, in her reply, said that what added to the satisfaction of receiving the proof of the Pope's kindness was, that it had been presented by a Nuncio to whose prudence Spain is indebted for signal benefits, and whom she and all her family cordially esteemed The King Consort also charged the Nuncio to express his gratitude to the Pope. Their Majesties then rose, and having the Nuncio on their right, proceeded to the Princess's apartment, where, after some religious ceremonies, the Nuncio put the blessed sash on the child's shoulders, and charged the governess, the .Marchioness of Povar, to watch diligentlv over her religious duties.

The Am azon. þÿ The arrival of the last West India steamer, without bringing any more news of the crew and passengers of the Amazon, and the announcement of the fact that the barque which was supposed to be near the burning ship, was spoken two days after the catastrophe, and communicated no intelligence that she had any of the missing crew or passengers on hoard, have almost destroyed the last vestige of hope that any more are saved. Mrs. Synions, the widow oft he unfortunate commander,

has left Southampton for Newcastle Iler brothers are some of the most eminent merchants in Jamaica. Miss Brady, the sister of the Admiralty agent is, it is feared, incurably afflicted. The shock and loss she has sustained have proved to much for her mind and frame. iMiss Smith, one of the passengers who was saved, and whose heroic conduct was the means of her own and other lives being preserved, is still at the Mayor of Southampton's residence at Winchester, where she has found a hospitable asylum. She has been treated with the utmost kindness also by the nobility, gentry, and clergy of the neighbourhood oi Winchester. She is occasionally aillicted with hysteric affections, the result ol great mental excitement and agony. A A Sunday or two ago a report was given out in Southampton that 26 more of the Amazon people had been saved. This report flew like wildfire through the town, and into the churches, from whence it was even announced from some of the pulpits. The friends and relatives of the lost were in a state of the greatest excitement, but the report turned out a cruel hoax. The Amazon fund now amounts to £9500.

Death of Marshal Marmont. þÿ Another ol Napoleon's favourite captainhas quitted the scene in which he has long ceased to sustain an active part The name ol Marshal Marmout w ill livr in association with those of Bernadottc Davoust, Lannes, and Berthier, Ins companions in arms, but Englishmen will especially remember it as that of a general most constantly found in opposition to our own commanders. Marmont was with Bonaparte in Egypt, and accompanied him, with Murat and Lannes, when he had resolved to quit the scene oi disaster. In the successtul campaign of I6U5, which ultimatcd in the peace ol Fresburg, Marmont commanded an army corps, and at its termination, having invaded the republic of Ragusa, and defeated the united Russians and Montenegrins in its neighbourhood, earned the the titular dignity which he hore till death. In 1612 we find him opposed to

W ellington in the Peninsula. He com manded at the battle of Salamanca, so honourable to the British arms, and there received a severe wound. In February, 1614, he was operating in conjunction with Mortier on the Marne for the de fence of the territory of France itself, and, being compelled to retreat, fell back upon Paris, March 2(1. Ten days afterwards lie was fain to capitulate to the allies, and on the 31 st of March marched out, of Paris. Marmont now took the oath to Louis XV1IL, and kept it when Bonaparte returned from Elba. It was his singular lot to have to surrender Paris a second time, namely, in 1630, when he had been entrusted by the reactionary Ministry of Charles X. with the command of all the troops. This may be considered the most interesting position which he occupied. The Nizam's Diamond. þÿ The Calcutta respondent at llydrabad : þÿ Englishman has the following from a cor- " The Nizarr

The Crystal I'alace. þÿ The following is the substance of a report made to the late Government by a committee appointed by the Lords of the Treasury to consider the question of the building. That committee consisted of three members þÿ Sir VV. Cubitt, Dr. Lindley, and Lord Seymour. They examined witnesses, and reported, we believe, in substance as follows : þÿ 1. That the Crystal I'a' ace, if retained, would cost <£200,000 to make it permanent, and adapt it for a winter garden, or repository of the arts and manufactures and other objects contemplated. 2. That if a portion of it were removed to Kew, it would entail an outlay of £30,000. 3. That a transposition to Battersea was not worthy ot serious consideration; and, lastly, that a structure better adapted for the purposes to which it was contemplated that the

Crystal Palace should be applied might be constructed at a smaller charge than the estimate of £200,000 specified. The committee give no positive opinion as to the retention or removal of the building. \s far as the Royal Commission are concerned, they have abandoned all idea of holding out a hand to help the inhabitants of the metropolis who are interested in this matter. Not only.is the building absolutely in the hands of the contractors, but the commissioners have issued orders to withdraw everything belonging to them. Their collection, which is to lor-m the groundwork of a trades' museum, is, in compliance with a decision come to on Monday, to be transferred to Kensington Palace, and in a tew days every vestige of their connexion with the Crystal Palace will have terminated.

Lamentations 2 c., (i v. ' The Lord hath caused the solemn feasts j and sabbaths to be forgotten in 'Awn:' Mr. Editor, þÿ I am constrained to add a few extra observations to what you | have already heard from inc, upon the profanation "of Sunday, which you will kindlv notice, on reading the above utterance of infallible truth. We may say what a dreadful thing sin is and how fast it brings desolation, is plainly ma- \ nifest from the history of Zion or Cod's ancient people. How deaf is the ear and hard the heart of man þÿ no example will , terrify þÿ no judgment hanging over his head, but arrested bv the hand of mercy, ! not, taste not, handle not the goods of will warn him of what God has done þÿ of what lie will do against sinners in general; against sabbath-breakers particularly. The command to remember the seventh day was forgotten in Israel, the rest of the sabbath was despised and God caused it to be so. As regards the present and the past this is a foul blot upon the Christian Zion and as respects the future, a different lot from God's people of old we cannot expect. To lend niv humble aid to avert this calamity I resume my pen, being satisfied I cannot confer a greater benefit upon all ranks of society than this, to cause them the sign of the sabbath þÿ by the help of the Mighty, a to recognise type and an earnest of the eternal rest that remaincth for the people of God. In this Island we are mixed community, professing different creeds, but many of us agreeing

the main articles of our faith. We profess to be Christians, called with an holy calling, after the very name of Him whose day the sabbath is; for we commemorate in it His glorious work, His signal triumph over thfe most deadly foes of our race. When we profane the sabbath we declare the victory is not for us, we eontcntlv remain under the curse, heaping up wrath against the great day of wrath; we deny that name which is our proud boast and with too daring a courage rob our Maker of that small portion of our time, which He claims for himself. Some of us say our sabbath begins at sun-down, others say at midnight þÿ in the use we differ, but in the abuse we differ not; our neighbours merely get the start of us a tew hours in profaning that da\ given by God that we might think hoiy thoughts and engage in holy acts to His honor and our own benefit. But is not this statement a tact, instead of the rest and holy quiet of sunday, we have the turmoil and discpiiet of the week ; instead of crowds of grateful and thankful worshippers in God's sanctuary, we have many there uncertain of what they would be at, many not there but filling the abodes of sin and idleness, many Sunday pleasurehunters, many sunday visitors, many engaged with the forbidden work oi the week, many keeping the poor working man from the consolations of religion to receive his weekly pay. I would suggest to the Police Masters the justice ol ordering the laborer who has to receive bis wages on a Sunday, a dav's pay 1 or at
least a part to compensate him tor the I J I loss of time, and his being compelled to forego the blessing of public worship.

Then we have the sunday bakers and the sunday-market frequenters, the sunday-storekeepers and the whole host of the devil's servants to be seen at every corner, to be met at every step, some of them fresh from the house of God, alter hearing that divine enactment (six days shalt thou labor and do all that thou hast to do), which the liberty or I should rather say, the licentiousness of the present age would dare to abrogate. It is the experience of men in the history of the world that when the restraint of the sabbath is removed it is hard to fix the point at which those vvlto are freed will stop, soon will they ripen for that awful recompense, which God will assuredly mete out to those under the curse of broken sabbaths; therefore let all remember lest God should cause you to forget. Remember to prepare for the duties of the sabbath ; remember that when you pray your spiritual and bodily existence depends upon the answer you receive; remember that when you praise God you cannot do so aright unless your interest in the blessed Saviour is undisputed. Fellow Islanders, þÿ remember to discourage and discountenance sabbathbreakers in every way you can. Touch

the Sunday-seller whether his door is whole, half or quarter open. Let Christians be ofone mind and of one spirit in this and at no distant day we will regain that which we have lost. By yielding to the utiholv practices of those who make a mock of sin, call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord honorable. Rejoice greatly when the work ol the week is done, that you may open a holy intercourse between you and your God in the peaceful ret i r < merit of the sanctuary. Pity and pray for those who know not one day from another þÿ like the men ol Ninevah of old who knew not tiieir right hand from their left, yet they repented at the preaching of Jonas. Behold a greater than Jona is here, who says to the sabbath break) r, ye bring evil upon the land. If the earth yields not her increase; if the clouds of Heaven give no rain ; if the sun of our prosperity sets finally ; il no blessing descends upon the labor of the husbandman ; let not us, as the fool, say in our hearts there is no God, !>nt confess, bewail and bemoan that we have caused the Lord to depart from us by dishonoring His holy day. It we act so, our Christianity is an empty title; our hope of happiness a vain delusion ; our profession gross hypocrisy; our attempts at serving God deceit, the evil of which will recoil upon the heads of those who use them. Be wise and hearken, your allegiance to the King of Heaven demands respect. Keep holy the sabbath day. It must grieve every subject of this King eternal that His au-

thority is held so cheap, while every diligence is used that the voice of man lie obeyed. þÿ cifixion a day on which much serious- This day is the vigil of the cruness becomes a Christian people. But there is no authority in the Bible, nor in the usage of the apostolic church to make it more holy than the Lord's day ; therefore 1 lament that some of the activity evinced by the authorities this day (Thursday) in shutting stores, stopping carts and hunting hreadsellcrs from the streets, is not bestowed, where it plight, in doing the same duty on Sunday. Take heed we do not bring upon ourselves the consequences of the fatal charge of those " Who changed the truth of God into a lie and worshipped and served the creature more than the creator who is blessed for ever." I remain, Mr. Editor, Your much obliged West- Ender. Thursday, April 8th 1852

Wilmer and Smith's European Tiiv March Hi, 1852 We alluded, some time ago, to tiic formation of an Irish company for the manufacture of beet-root sugar in tin sister-kingdom. This company, which consists mainly of London capitalists, has already commenced operations at Mount Mellick, in Queen's County, and may now be said to be in working trim It has already received a charter of in corporation, and, as the company has plenty of capital, it can command skill and may possibly prove pecuniarily productive. The amount of unemployed capital in the British metropolis, which is always seeking for any profitable in vestment, leaves no kind of doubt that if the speculation should succeed, it will be followed by similar undertakings Some time must necessarily elapse be fore sufficient data can be obtained on which to base permanent calculations; but, hitherto, the proprietors seem t<> have gone about this work in an earnest spirit, and, judging by what has been done, there are evidently practical men connected with the undertaking, whose sole object will be to make the under taking remunerative. This new company has not trusted to such unskilled labour as they could pro cure in Ireland. They have gone to Belgium for their workmen, who have been transplanted to Queen's Count, and with the new hands have been com bined a number of natives, who w ill be taught by the foreigners everv necessan essential in the way of extracting from the beet-root the greatest amount of saccharine matter. Belgium, beyond any other European country, has become

famous tor its beet-root sugar. The chemists of that country, as we have before mentioned, have had their atten t ion devoted to the subject by strong pecuniary inducements, and the resul lias been considerable improvements in the mode of producing t Ire article, ac companied, as in all such eases, by great er economy, the result, of superior skill. It is stated that the Irish beet-root is the best which can be found for the purpose of extraction. Fifteen tons of beet will yield a ton of sugar, and as the con sumption of Ireland is calculated at 50,000 tons annually, it follows that 750,000 tons ol'the root will be required tor this purpose. It is useless to disguise the fact that tiris experiment will meet with the approval of all who are interested in the prosperity of Ireland ; and. if the specu l:it ion can be made to pay, there are sufficient inducements, as we have said, to greatly extend a trade which will introduce British capital into the sister country. The amount of wages which the new undertaking will distribute, is in itself a very important element, and cannot fail to benefit a country the poverty of which is unhappily notorious. Employment in the cultivation of the root w ill progress in proportion to the success which may attend the development of this novel scheme, and if that success realises one-half of the glowing pictures which certain parties are now engaged in painting, the material prosperity of Ireland cannot fail to feel its influence. This intelligence cannot be very grati-

fying to our West Indian readers ; but, as they have been previously prepared for it, it will not come upon them unexpectedly. One of the laws of to social ex istence is a constant exposure compe t i t ion of every kind, and those who profit by improvements are not over anxious to inquire how many are thereby injured. During the last eighteen years the West Indies have become familiarised with misfortunes and disasters of every kind

and, although the production of the Irish beet-root is hardly likely to prove ' the last straw which breaks the camel's hack," it must add, more or less, to that competition to which they, beyond any other class in connexion with the British Crown, have been subjected. The remedy will be found, not in a subject of despondency, and a wish to quit the field, but in a resolute determination to make the most of circumstances, and by the introduction of every scientific improvement, to give to the tropical cane a fair chance in the race of competition. In some of t lie islands the introduction of new machinery of recent years has been general, and it is possible that this may be carried out to a still greater extent. We know sanguine West Indians who apprehend no fear from the production of beet-root sugar in the mother country. All they ask for is a sufficient quantity of free labour to face the opposition which surrounds them. In this request there is surely nothing unreasonable. Such a demand, urged with all the potent reasoning by which it can be supported, ought to tell upon the Government which is now in power, and which in opposition professed to be moved with strong sympathies for the isles ol the W est. The time seems opportune for drawing the attention of the new ministry to this important phase of the question, in that direction the chances of immediate success seem greater than in any other. None of the difficulties which attach to differential suirar duties here interpose, and the op-
position which on most other points would be formidable, would on this be weak and inconsiderable.

Communications. Mr. Editor, Dear Sir ! þÿ Allow mo to make a few remarks on the subject of Militia duty ; but in so doing, i would wish it to bo distinctly understood, that it is not my intention to recommence the squabble on this subject, whicli took place some tune ago. Last Saturday, the miserable remnant of the Burgher Corps met, according to summons, for the purpose of being drilled and to have their arms examined. They however escaped a drilling by being so few. Now sir, I cannot but wonder at the injustice of such an act as this. All who now do Militia-duty compose but a small portion of the inhabitants who should do this duty. Still, the majority are never summoned to do so, but we are obliged þÿ for no other reason, I can conceive, than to prevent our officers from losing their practice in field-tactics. The few men composing the wretched corps, could never answer the purpose of a Militia force, audi therefore ask why are we not granted a temporary exemption until the reorganisation, which is under never-ending consideration, take place. Is it just that one inhabitant shall be obliged, and be fined if he refuses, to do Militia-duty, while another may be entirely freo of this duty ? I am here reminded of an order from the Stadshauptmancy, published in October last year, calling upon all persons, under pain of a fine, to report themselves within eight days after their arrival here, in order that they may be enrolled in the Militia. On the publication of this order, we began to enter-

tain hope that the authorities intended to turn their at. tention to the Militia; but how disappointed were we, when we understood, that on many individuals calling at this office, for the pur|Kise as stated in the advertisement, they were told that they might remain as before, until further notice. In the hope that an equal division of Militia labour will soon be made, and that we, the present sufferers, may soon be able to realize the consolation held out in the following lines, " Company in distress Makes the trouble less," i remain, dear Sir Yours »

Mr. Editor, þÿ Among the ex traordi nary and absurd things one meets with in life, it would he hard to find a parallel for the proposition contained in an advertisement in your gazette of Friday last, viz : that we should fish up, out ot our poorly, alas ! very poorly furnished purses, some dollars to erect an Ebenezer in the Spanish Capital. Though grave in character I cannot refrain a smile; for I thought ofthe maxim, Charity begins at home. Are there not countless objects in our Island, where our spare money may he bestowed with advantage ? Are there not countless calls, which it is our duty to listen to? We are introducing a new system of cultivating the ground. Extend this improvement to the great moral field, that surrounds us ; pull up the noxious weeds ; stir the barren and neglected soil ; think of the hands that have fiHed your pockets with money; give some of it back to fill their heads with knowledge, their hearts with truth ; shew your gratitude to the

God of Heaven, not for a single favour, (like what the Spaniards conferred upon you, in which self was deeply concerned,) but for benefits without number, which he lias bestowed. The hurricane, the earthquake and the pestilence have been called to punish guilty lands, while we have been spared. Here is a call to graþÿtitude upon this foundation raise an Ebenezer in the way 1 recommend, not in Madrid, but in Santa Croix, then you will have something to contemplate with satisfaction ; but if the Spanish Capital has a prior claim upon your benevolence, your gullibility will render you objects of pity to the foreigners who pocket your Cash. Mr. Editor, your obliged Wesl-Ender. April 19th 1652.

Swimming. þÿ The following is given as the rationale of swimming. No branch of education has been so much neglected as this. Man is the only animal which does not swim naturally. He sinks in deep water from the size of his brain when not properly exercised. That is to say the weight of his brain above his nose, sinks that organ a little beneath the surface, when he is in an erect position, before his body displaces its weight in water, and thus finds an equilibrium. With the nose under, one must breathe water and drown. But when the brain becomes to be exercised enough to throw the head back aiuLthe nose up, pointing to and the feet very zeijth, and keep the hands carefully under water, then by the eternal laws of hydrostatics, the nose will continue above water, and the person will float like an empty bottle which is so balanced as to keep its mouth uppermost. St. Thomas Times, 10 th April 1852. We have been requested to five publicity to the following letter from Jos- \ DeGout, Esq., to the President of the British Virgin Islands, communicating particulars of the late destructive conflagration at St. þÿ Honor's reply : Bartholomew, with Ilis To His Honor I.ieutenant-Colonel Chads, President Administering the Government of the British Virgin Islands, Ate., &.c., atc. St. Thomas, 16th March. 1852 Sir þÿ The lamentable character of this communication will, I hope, prove a sufficient apology for the liberty I assume in submitting a statement of the same to the considerate attention of Your Honor. On the 2nd instant, the principal portion of the 3rd section of the Town of Gustavia, in the Swedish Island of St. Bartholomew, was destroyed by a conflagration, which commenced at 2 o'clock in the morning; the flames spread with such violence and rapidity that the Morning Sun rose over the smoking ruins of Two hundred Buildings, and a BEG- GAR'D PEOPLE! the hapless inhabitants driven by the lire from house to house, thence to the beach, and as many as the vessels could give shelter to were | taken on board, ltich and poor have been crushed, and their ruin completed. They abandoned all they possessed, and the sentiments of self-preservation, for the ties of kindred, proved superior to all consideration of property or interest. By this awful visitation, a People within a few miles of our shores have been, and are at this moment, reduced to the greatest distress þÿ respectable fami-

lies, mothers, widows and orphans, are involved in a common ruin. On the announcement here of the calamity, and the distressing situation of the sufferers, I addressed an Appeal to the Inhabitants of St. Thomas, who have with their usual liberality contributed a handsome amount for the temporary relief of the victims. I have already dispatched a communication to His Excellency the Governor of St. Bartholomew, wherein the conduct of this community is recorded, announcing the amount of $1,600 held by me, and subject to his orders. Further efforts are about being made by some of the most influential inhabitants here to increase, if possible, the means of relief. In behalf of the sufferers, I now address an " Appeal to the Inhabitants of Tortola." I respectfully solicit that Your Honor will graciously open the List of Subscribers, and thus offer an example of that sympathy which extraordinary misfortunes will invariably create in the breasts of men alive to the calls of humanity. , I have the honor to be, Sir, Your Honor's most obdt. sevt., JOS. DeGOUT.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avit. Sir! þÿ Through the politeness of an obliging friend, a hook was sent me the other day, hearing on its hack in gilt letiritk St. Croix and St. Johns ters the high sounding title : " St. Thomas ." On looking sit its title ptige, i find it to tie written by a person calling himself, the "Pastor ot the Reformed Dutch Church St. Thomas." As to the general contents of the book þÿ its arrangement and historical accuracy, I do not intend to say much. In truth, front the very first page to the last, it falls so short, of any thing, that ordinarily comes under the established laws, either of history or criticism ; that 1

© 'is © 3 «£ AT would never have done, Were I to pursue the countless blunders it contains. There is one particular defect, however, to which 1 beg to direct the attention of your readers; as it singularly illustrates that hostility, which loves to shew its teeth against the Church ol God ; even although it cannot bite. At page 120, the author in speakingof thelnsurrection of 1848, remarks; " that the slaves teas "(elr/) " violence in impelled not the destruction of property to greater acts of "etc., is only to he accounted for by the "power which Christianity influenced "over them, through the labours of the "Moravian, Episcopal and Lutheran "clergymen." þÿ The remainder of the sentence is so unworthy of even the commonest school boy þÿ that 1 suppress it, and refer the reader to the precious original itself. This opinion, given as the "deliberate opinion" of the author, contains not only an indirect insult to the Catholic clergy and people of this island ; hut it involves also a suppression of the truth, for which nothing hut ignorance or the rankest bigotry can account. The writer must he aware, that the Catholic labourers of this Island form no inconsiderable portion of the population. In the struggle for liberty, they were implicated as well as others of the different denominations; if then they had at their mercy, the lives of those, whom they formerly obeyed þÿ if they obtained possession of so much property, and yet destroyed so little; I cannot for the life of me, see, how this is to lie attributed to

the teaching of the ministers of the Moravian, Episcopal or Lutheran congregations. The Catholic slaves here were never under the guidance of any other teachers but their own priests þÿ the teaching which they received, and still continue to receive is as perfect, if not more so than that, afforded by any other of the different denominations. Not only it embraces sermons and lectures, lessons and reading from the sacred scriptures, hut together with this, the Catholic priest is continually engaged one way or the other in attending to the instruction of his people; this moment he hears a complaint, he reconciles the contending parties and sends them away in peace; the next moment he is preparing some poor soul for its passage to eternity ; in every place and at every time, the people have free access to his council þÿ they lay hefore him their doubts þÿ they expose to him their wants þÿ they look upon him as their father and their friend. And in what I ask have they ever been deceived, that would cause them to have recourse to the teaching of other men? There can he nothing more absurd, than such a supposition. Had the author taken the trouble of enquiring of some of our enlightened planters, as to the manner in which the Catholic slaves Were instructed, he would have found, that during the time of slavery, no ordinary pains were taken to make them good and faithful servants, and to impress them with the idea that they were not so much the servants of men, but rather

serving their great master in Heaven. As to the revolution itself to which the author alludes, had he asked the question, he would have found that the Catholic Priests did not abandon their people in the moment of danger ; on the contrary, they went amongst them; they raised their voiceagainst theirexcesses, wherever they found them; they begged; they supplicated thern, as well asothcrs, to retire peaceably to their homes, and to abstain from every infringement of the law. It is true, that the fruit of all this instruction may not have been as great as they themselves desired; lint then could it he otherwise? Or does the history of Revolutions, and more particu-

larly the revolution of a slave population, struggling for freedom, and maddened by drink, effort! us a solitary example of a people, throwing down their arms and humbly submitting to the teaching ol the Gospel under such circumstances. It would indeed he an unheard-of prodigy in the History of the world. More than this; the author will learn for his better information, that after the Insurrection, the Catholic Priests did every thing in their power, to discover if any ot their people still retained any portion of their master's property, and wherever it was found, that even a common glass, or cup, was not restored to its lawful owner, they interposed their authority and saw (at least as far as in them lay) that justice was done. 1 his looks something like Evangelical teaching, and for this teaching the people are indebted to no others, hut to their own pastors. All this, it is impossible, that the author could he ignorant ot had he taken the trouble to make the necessary inquiries. But the fact is this, lie wanted a lling at the Catholic Reliþÿgion It " is thy name, that is my enemy ;" and therefore to indulge his taste, he takes to the old hncknied hug-bears, by which the terror of so many past generations have been kept alive. As his hook could lay claim to no great novelty, the old stuff required some seasoning ; hence, his invidious suppression of the truth. But, on the other hand, insinuations like to that, thrown out by the author, are as harmless a

the noxious little insects, of which he tells us (page 219) » that the ling of the one is easily removed, and that the sting ol the other proved a very trifling affair." Really now is it so? I would strongly recommend our Author, if ever he hopes that his book will see a second edition, to collect some more correct information than that with which he is at present supplied. Our Jiggers here, it would appear, are much more formidable than those in St. Thomas. Does the Parson know, that it is not a thing of very rare occurrence, that some of our people of the cleanliest habits are sometimes laid up, for weeks together, after the Jigjrer and his hag have been removed. We have examples even of persons having lost their lives, in consequence of the inflammation caused by some of those poisonous intruders. The Scorpions and Centipedes too, seem to have a little more pluck in them than those of the Sister Island (page 219) ; for it is not uncommon in St. Croix that the sting of a Scorpion or Centipede should give fever, and cause a disagreeable nausea to the stomach. Those things, trifling as they are, the author should know þÿ ignorance of them in him is unpardonable. When next he revises his hook, and indeed it requires revision, I hope he will tell the truth þÿ the whole truth þÿ and suppress no portion of it. Let him give the very Inserts their due! Should lie want to make out a strong case þÿ something that would excite a little more sympathy for a man, living in the tropics with the thermometer raging

continuously, day and night, at 82 degrees (and that is no joke) þÿ let linn senil over to St. Croix, and we will send liini a cock and a lien (a pair I mean) of the real breed of our obnoxious insects; otherwise, when people read his book they will open their eyes and stare, and, throwing it down, they will exclaim with a hearty laugh ; the History of St. Thomas with St. Croix and St. Johns is yet to he written. Wishing the Author better luck in his next literary effort, I hid him a respectful adieu ; requesting him, henceforward, always to bear in mind that "One story's good till another is told" GAMMA.

to our number of tne 20th instant we inserted an article, the object of which our readers will have seen by this, is nothing 'ess, than to dissuade the inhabitants of this Island, from responding to the appeal made to triein through Major Keutsch, in behalf of certain countable objects for the capital of Spain þÿ the article to which we refer is signed " Westender." This grave person, who smiles occasionally ; but scarcely ever laughs, we suppose, tells us that we are called upon to ' fish up out of our poorly, alas ! very poorly furnished purses, some dollars to erect an Ebenezer in the Spanish capital." He appears indignant at the idea of such a profane waste, and from his appeal to our pockets, one might judge, that it was our poverty, which was the reason why we should not contribute to this charitable purpose. But poor simpletons ! all our doubts are dissipated, when a little further on, we are told, onr pockets are so full that we onght to open them and give back some of the overflowing mammon, to fill the peoples heads with knowledge. A very important advice this no doubt ; but ye wise logicians of old, who toiled so long over the midnight lamp, will you condescend to inform us by what sleight of hand a man whose purse is " poorly, alas ! very poorly furnished," can, at the same moment find it so " full," that he has nothing to do, but to shake out its exuberance, to fill peoples heads with knowledge. Perhaps we do not understand this grave person, who speaks thus mysti-

cally ; and therefore leaving him to explain himself on thiB point, we must do him the justice to say, that he attempts to give us another reason, why we should not contribute to this charitable appeal. The Spaniards, he says, conferred only a single favor on us, and in that favor Self was deeply concerned. We must confess that the very contrary appears to us to be the truth. But even supposing for a moment that the Spanish Government did act on the principle, that when a man sees his neighbour's house on fire, it is time for him to look to his þÿown what wc ask has this to do with the important services, which the Spanish troops rendered in the hour of danger ? Look also to the manner in which those services were rendered. The Spanish troops did not come here, as they might have done, to be billeted on the hospitality of the community; they brought wi'h them their owr doubloons, to the

3 tr . e m <o a x 1 - a t a a. | amount of nearly fifty thousand dollars, and even to the commonest necessaries for an encampment, they were well and efficiently supplied. How then can our Correspondent have the boldness to assert, that Self was the motive, which induced the Spaniards to come to our assistance ; or how can he attempt to raise his voice to dissuade the community from responding to the appeal which has been made to us ? Had he been in Basin 011 the morning of the day, which brought ihe Spanish troops to this Island, he would have witnessed a spectacle well calculated to excite the sympathy of the hardest heart. Here, on one side, he would have seen, children and delicate females, hastening through the streets, with throbbing hearts, to join their friends, on board the vessels in the harbour. There, on the other side, he would have seen the old and the infirm, wending their way to the Fort, carrying with them whatever was most precious of their household þÿ all this and more, he would have witnessed. But behold ! how in a few moments the scene alters. A c'oud of smoke is seen from afar þÿ hundreds of anxious eyes are directed towards the spot þÿ what can it be ? is anxiously asked. It is a steamer ! they say ; and so it is þÿ onward she comesþÿ she rides gallantly up to the harbour's mouth þÿ the people are elevated with joy þÿ their fears are þÿdissipated they recognise the men, who cotne to protect them þÿ never will we forget the tranquility that followed from that moment. The people returned to

their homes, with joyful hearts, and that night was a blessed night ol repose to many a wearied limb. Shall we allude to the subsequent conduct of the Spanish soldiers, during the time they remained 111 the Island ? It is unnecessary. Suffice it to say, that tlie officers were gentlemen, and as to the privates, tlieir conduct and discipline inspired every one with perlect confidence. It our Correspondent wee acquainted witii those facts, he would have saved himself the trouble of rushing into print. We are therefore reluctantly obliged to denounce his communication as unmanly, ungenerous and narrow-minded, and we only hope, that it will not dissuade one single individual from responding to the appeal, which has been made to us. It the matter is to stand or tall, let it be on its ®wn merit ; hut justice as well as gratitude require that no one should prejudge the case.
